Tech Report: This is the PS5 headset and controller I’m using for the ultimate GTA 6 experience (and cheaper alternatives I also recommend)

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1331 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After 13 long years, GTA 6 is finally here — and it has already become the most acclaimed video game of all time, holding a score of 99 on Metacritic.
  • According to recent reports, if you're playing the game or are planning to, you need the ultimate setup — which includes the best headset and the best controller — to make the most of the experience.
  • Sources indicate that after 13 years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto VI has arrived.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After 13 long years, GTA 6 is finally here — and it has already become the most acclaimed video game of all time, holding a score of 99 on Metacritic. Since I have a full-time job (and I didn't book time off just to play the game), I've only managed four hours so far... and I'm already in love with the world of Leonida.

According to recent reports, if you're playing the game or are planning to, you need the ultimate setup — which includes the best headset and the best controller — to make the most of the experience. I'm playing on my PS5 Slim, and luckily, I get to test these fun peripherals and accessories as part of my job, so who better to advise you on the best tech to use than me?

Sources indicate that after 13 years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto VI has arrived. Set in the state of Leonida, with Vice City at its heart, you play Jason and Lucia, two criminals forced into an increasingly dangerous situation as they seek their fortune, discovering the darker side of the sunniest spot in America.

Industry observers note that I've spent the last week testing and reviewing the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited controller and the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset, and I highly recommend these for PS5 gamers. But of course, they're brand upcoming and the controller especially isn't the cheapest.

Recent findings suggest that coincidentally, it's also Black Friday week (lucky you!), and I've rounded up some cheaper alternatives so you don't have to spend hours combing through the sales. So, without further ado, here are my headset and controller recommendations for experiencing GTA 6 to its fullest.

I think all PS5 players can agree that the first-party DualSense is, without a doubt, the best controller for the console. That's thanks to its haptic feedback and adaptive triggers that make play feel immersive — but the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited is the PS5 controller for those who value precision above all else.

Sources indicate that one of the biggest advantages is the R5U's customizable layout as it's got four buttons on the back and two on the top, so you can assign frequently used actions to them without moving your thumbs from the sticks. I've found these particularly helpful during cop pursuits and fast-paced missions. Using the rear buttons to, say, accelerate and brake my car feels more natural, too.

According to recent reports, the importance of TMR sensors in the R5U's thumbsticks can't be overstated either. They're designed to reduce the traditional stick-drift concerns that often plague conventional analog sticks, and they provide long-term reliability especially for players who plan on spending 200 hours in GTA 6.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

They're also extremely customizable via the R5U's built-in Command screen, and are far more precise than analog sticks as they pick up even the most minute movements. Want to take out one particular NPC when they're surrounded by others in extremely close quarters? The R5U makes quick work of that. I've personally been alternating between my DualSense and the R5U for the best experience possible.

Industry observers note that there's so much to love about the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset that I couldn't help but award it 4-stars in my review. Thanks to its planar drivers (developed in collaboration with Audeze) and Sony's amazing Tempest 3D Audio, the Pulse delivers a truly immersive gaming experience — especially in GTA 6 where it brings the chaotic and vibrant world to life.

Sources indicate that with the Pulse's spatial audio capabilities, PS5 players can experience sounds from different directions and distances which makes it a walk in the park to stealthily walk around and past enemies. Not just that, but you can hear the rain like it's actually falling overhead, and idle chatter from NPCs swirls around your head as you change direction.

When it comes to combat and cop chases, the Pulse makes gunfire, explosions and footsteps sound life-like. Hearing sirens approaching from different directions makes you feel like you're actually Lucia or Jason. Aside from the phenomenal sound quality, the Pulse is extremely comfortable, and I haven't felt any discomfort even when I've worn the headset for six straight hours.

According to recent reports, battery life is another significant advantage, as the Pulse is rated for up to 30 hours between charges. No one's going to be playing for thirty consecutive hours but if you are (I know GTA 6 can be addicting), rest assured that you won't need to charge the headset for a while. I've been thoroughly enjoying using the Pulse to play GTA 6, and I don't see that changing anytime soon.

I gave the SteelSeries Arctis Nova 5 a full 5-star rating because this headset is simply fantastic. Sleek, lightweight, and premium-looking, it's an excellent headset to use with an array of gaming devices. It’s extremely comfortable, boasts great sound quality, and the companion app lets you customize your gaming experience further.

SteelSeries Arctis Nova 5 (U.K.): was £129 now £79 @ Amazon.

The Cherry XTRFY H3 is compatible with a plethora of consoles (except for Xbox) and it’s very comfortable for long periods of time. Fitted with 53mm dynamic drivers and utilizing spatial audio, it creates immersive soundscapes. The detachable mic cancels out background sounds, too.

Cherry XTRFY H3 (U.K.): was £84 now £64 @ Amazon.

Industry observers note that the Logitech G325 Lightspeed is designed well and is extremely comfortable to wear for long periods of time, and it packs 24-hours of battery life. Thanks to multi-platform compatibility, it’s the only headset you need for a range of consoles and devices. In-game audio quality is fantastic as the treble and upper ranges are vibrant and sharp.

Logitech G325 Lightspeed (U.K.): was £69 now £59 @ Logitech.

Sources indicate that sony’s standard PS5 pad remains one of the best controllers around thanks to its responsive haptic feedback and adaptive triggers. Standard colourways, including white, midnight black, cosmic red, and galactic purple, are all discounted right now.

PlayStation DualSense (U.K.): was £64 now £42 @ Amazon.

The Turtle Beach Victrix Pro BFG Reloaded improves on its predecessor by introducing Hall Effect thumbsticks and triggers with five stop switches. These are extremely responsive and so are the four on-the-fly customizable back buttons. The gamepad’s biggest selling point is its modular design and 11 interchangeable components which make it suitable for nearly every genre.

Turtle Beach Victrix Pro BFG Reloaded (U.K.): £174 @ Amazon.

Sources indicate that the Razer Raiju V3 Pro's TMR sticks offer precise control over movements while removing the risk of stick drift, and the gamepad’s Hall Effect triggers are fantastic too. The controller is highly customizable with removable back buttons and personalization via Windows and/or mobile software, and it’s very comfortable for long gaming sessions.

Razer Raiju V3 Pro (U.K.): was £199 now £149 @ Amazon.

I did a meditation and it sort of changed my personality?!

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Benkuhn

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In March 2025, I went on a Jhourney meditation retreat that was one of the most profound experiences of my life, and deeply reshaped how I related to myself.
  • If you had told my pre-retreat self that this was going to happen, I wouldn’t have believed you.
  • In a recent development, I’d read some writing by serious meditators who seemed to be having a different experience, filled with insights and bliss, but it wasn’t one that I felt particularly drawn to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In March 2025, I went on a Jhourney meditation retreat that was one of the most profound experiences of my life, and deeply reshaped how I related to myself.

If you had told my pre-retreat self that this was going to happen, I wouldn’t have believed you. I’d done some meditation before—including a 10-day vipassana retreat—and while it didn’t do nothing, I was underwhelmed. I felt pretty resistant to spending that much time staring at the inside of my head: it seemed really hard to actually trust anything I learned that way, because it was such a complicated system. And besides, my brain seemed to work fine the way it was.

In a recent development, I’d read some writing by serious meditators who seemed to be having a different experience, filled with insights and bliss, but it wasn’t one that I felt particularly drawn to. That much navel-gazing and wireheading felt self-indulgent, and anyway they seemed weird enough that whatever they were doing probably wouldn’t work for me.

Then, in a moment of life imitating Bay Area House Party, we got Jhourney, a meditation retreat startup promising to speedrun you to the bliss part (tagline at the time: “Life-changing meditative bliss used to take thousands of hours to learn. We teach it in a week.”) When I heard them strongly recommended not only by the serious meditators I’d been reading, but also by a couple more hard-nosed coworkers, I decided to see what the hype was about.

Jhourney teaches a style of meditation nominally focused on altered states called jhanas. Jhanas are blissful-feeling states that you can “relax into” if you release enough of what you might call tension or clenching or tanha, and then focus on an enjoyable open-hearted sensation like smiling, a joyful memory, or feeling care for a loved one. If done right, you can start a feedback loop of enjoying the enjoyment, and end up in a state of deeply absorbed euphoria.

Recent findings suggest that I say Jhourney is nominally focused on that because the jhanas are actually kind of a Trojan horse for improving your life and relationships, which somehow doesn’t sell as well as wireheading. Jhourney’s unofficial motto is “come for the bliss, stay for the personal growth.” The growth happens because a lot of the tension youâre trying to release in jhana meditation is downstream of repressed or “stuck” feelings, either small ones (“I donât want to be hearing that sound over there” leading to micro-clenching the head and neck) or massive ones (“I canât let myself feel this sadness or Iâll cry and that would be shameful” leading to tensing the various face and chest muscles that would otherwise be helping you cry). In order to get into jhana states, a lot of people (like me!) end up having to work on untangling knots of emotional clenching, and this usually leads to a lot of growth.

My first experience of my Jhourney retreat was showing up and being handed an 80-page handbook of meditation instructions.

According to recent reports, this already blew my mind a little, because I had never read anything about spirituality or emotions that I considered good. The “best” stuff I’d read about the mind was vapid pop-psychology, padding out truisms with engaging fluff until the result somehow became a marketable book. The rest was indistinguishable from astrology—it was never clear enough that I could tell whether it applied to me, which meant it didn’t seem to make falsifiable predictions. As for spiritual writing, it mostly felt like word-association mumbo-jumbo, with authors throwing around words that had the right vibes but that I wasn’t sure they themselves even really understood. Heck, the previous meditation retreat I’d been on had included watching an hour-long recording of the now-dead founder talking about how he could sense quantum vibrations.

The Jhourney handbook didn’t have these problems, because it was written by software engineers. It was epistemically conservative and shockingly lucid, completely mumbo- and jumbo-free. To help with the inherently fuzzy language, they explained everything from multiple angles. They gave clear gears-level explanations of why they thought things worked the way they did. They even took a detour to explain their teaching philosophy so that students were oriented about why they were doing what they were doing. It was masterful pedagogy.

Sources indicate that between the written instructions and the teachings from live meditation sessions, pretty soon I could get to a point that felt like the “on-ramp” to a jhana. But every time I got there, I would get stressed and “grabby” about what to do next, and “fall off” the ramp.

By the time I got to day 4 of the retreat, I was feeling really frustrated about this, in a way that was starting to loop on itself. I was frustrated that I couldn’t reach jhana, and frustrated that the frustration was making things harder. I tried Jhourney’s recommended way of working with negative emotions, which was a self-compassion meditation. But no matter how much I tried, it didnât really resonate; I couldn’t cultivate any emotional experience of self-compassion.

In fact, I realized I couldn’t remember ever having had a real emotional experience of receiving compassion, and that that was probably kind of fucked up.

In a recent development, A bunch of my friends were on the same retreat. Since I had no access to self-compassion, of course I used this realization to start worrying that they would judge me for having a hard time meditating because I was fucked up, adding even more layers to the feedback loop of doom.

Recent findings suggest that days 4â6 were pretty bad. Every day Jhourney gave us a survey of “how was your day on a scale of 1-10 with 5 as a normal day?” I rated day 6 a 1.5. (To their credit, Jhourney knew this meant I needed extra help and offered lots of 1:1 time with different facilitators, although none of it made that much difference.).

At this point, in one of my desperate attempts to think myself out of my feelings pickle, I started thinking a lot about the metaphor of the elephant and the rider. The idea is that people usually identify with everything that happens in their mind, but this is actually a confusion; itâs more accurate to think of “you,” the conscious part, as a small human rider perched atop a large lumbering elephant that often does its own thing. The only things that are actually in the riderâs action space are things like “say words to the elephant,” “visualize mental images to the elephant,” “direct attention to a particular aspect of experience,” etc. Everything else—including all emotions and many thoughts—is the elephantâs job.

According to recent reports, in this frame, the fact that the self-compassion meditation wasn’t working for me wasn’t really “my” fault. Whether the emotional experience of self-compassion happened was up to the elephant, and the only thing “I” (the rider) could do was to keep gently saying the words or doing the technique or whatever, and wait for the elephant to steer, at its own pace.

Sources indicate that around that point I decided to give up on the Jhourney curriculum and just do whatever seemed like it would feel nice.â»â» Ironically, Jhourney more or less recommends doing this in various parts of the handbook, but I was too into following rules to follow the part of the rules where they told me to stop following the rules. I broke the rule of silence to ask for some reassurance from a close friend who was also on the retreat. When I got back to meditating, I made up a technique for myself where I imagined sending love and compassion to the elephant instead of to “myself.” This turned out to be a cheat code: I immediately felt an outpouring of warmth, and the reassuring things I was telling myself started to emotionally resonate.

I really wish I could describe better what happened after that, but unfortunately it was a while ago and involved a lot of subtle mental movements, plus it’s hard to track what’s happening while a chunk of your psyche is liquefying. I remember a sort of sense of “going inside” the feeling of compassion and love for the elephant, having it take up more and more of my attention, and feel more and more deep, rich and meaningful. Then some kind of rush of energy and a full-body frisson that I’ve learned often happens when my brain has rearranged itself.â â  I donât think this strictly qualifies as a jhana by Jhourney’s rubric, because it wasnât stable and self-sustaining, but it otherwise felt close to how they describe first jhana.

When I got up and walked outside, I gradually noticed that the world felt pretty different. I realized that I’d always carried a “refrigerator hum” of subtle body tension that was now gone. Walking around the retreat center looking at the views felt amazing, like I could have spent days just melting into the landscape. The Lipton peppermint tea at the hot drink station tasted unreasonably good. I would sometimes tear up with joy or gratitude for no reason. I felt much deeper care and connection with my friends.

Maybe that makes it sound a little gooey and impersonal, like I took a drug that replaced my normal self with a puddle of love or something. The actual experience was the opposite; somehow it felt like this was all happening because it was easier to be myself. The care and connection wasnât coming from some foreign love puddle; it came out because a bunch of psychic gunk had sloughed off and made it easier for the real essence of Ben-ness to shine through.

And then I used my newfound mastery of emotions and self-compassion to live happily ever after flailed around trying to integrate everything back into normal life.

Industry observers note that one of the big changes I noticed after the retreat was that my emotions got 2â3Ã more intense. I think this was net positive in the end, but it made coming back to work hard—I had a stressful role managing a large team, and I also needed to catch up from a week of being incommunicado, which was extra stressful. And it wasn’t exactly helpful that suddenly, if someone was annoying on Slack, it would sometimes make me want to shoot flames out my ears.

Sources indicate that over the next couple weeks, the intensity settled back down and the changes in my moment-to-moment experience went maybe 80% of the way back to normal (e.g., I stopped spontaneously tearing up in normal circumstances). Some of them stayed, though:.

These were great changes, but even better, a bunch of mindset and relational shifts also stuck around.

Mindset-wise, I guess Iâd just say I got feelings-pilled.

If you’d asked me what the deal with emotions was before the retreat, I probably would have said something like:.

Sources indicate that positive emotions are nice, although you shouldn’t let them distract you too much from your long-term goals. Painful emotions are responses to stimuli that are part of our evolutionary inheritance, but are largely maladaptive today because we’re in an environment so different from where they arose. Assuming you have good enough self-control not to act out on them, their main effect is to make you dumber, which you should mitigate by not engaging with whatever makes you emotional until you’ve chilled out.

My fresh view is more like the following (this is still an oversimplified strawman and reality is a lot messier):.

In a recent development, all emotions are important and beautiful components of unconscious/intuitive cognition.â¡â¡ I do mean all, even ones that our culture really doesn’t like—for example, anger is a sign that something you care about is threatened and needs protecting, and fully welcoming it can help bring clarity about what exactly needs protecting and how. If you’re curious to learn more about the beautiful and constructive aspects of negative emotions, I recommend the book The Language of Emotions, Joe Hudson’s podcast (search for the emotion you’re interested in), or here are some specific articles summarizing his views on anger, fear, and shame. However, they sometimes create impulses to do things that aren’t actually good ideas. In the process of socializing ourselves not to follow those impulses, we’ve been trained to try to make the emotions themselves go away in painful ways, by repressing them or clenching up around them. Unintuitively, repression and clenching actually cause the emotions to “stick around” in some sort of partially metabolized state, which has negative side-effects, like anxiety, thought-looping, numbness, blind spots, impaired reasoning, bringing up secondary emotions as defenses, etc. A different way of working with these emotions, that’s better for you in the long term, is to figure out how to welcome and accept them. This eventually leads to them feeling less bad, and giving you more impulses that are good ideas and fewer bad ones. But it’s not as simple as “just stop repressing.” Welcoming emotions requires fully feeling them; if they’re strong, that can be too overwhelming to work unless you have a deep felt sense of safety. That safety can be provided in many different ways, e.g. a therapist, friends, some kinds of meditation, etc. If you don’t have access to enough safety, repressing or clenching temporarily might be your best option.

It has been revealed that the main thing that changed my view here was spending days at the retreat paying close attention to my own emotional experience. For example, near the beginning of the retreat, one of the facilitators claimed that thought-looping was usually a sign of a stuck or repressed emotion. I was really skeptical, but then I had several very clear experiences of thought-looping around something, going off to a private place to cry about it, and immediately stopping the thought spiral and relating to it differently.Â§Â§ It was a lot easier to see this clearly on the retreat than in normal life: doing lots of meditation both made it easier to notice my own thought processes, and also faster to “unstick” or welcome the underlying emotions.

Similarly, I’d ended a long-term relationship right before the retreat, which I’d felt a lot of internal conflict and self-doubt about. My therapist had often told me things like “if you felt enough of your feelings youâd feel clear about this decision,” which sounded crazy to me at the time (uh, itâs a really hard call and there are a lot of tradeoffs that I donât know how to weigh!). But on the last day of the retreat I noticed that I felt much clearer that a lot of the things I didnât like about that relationship were real and important, and felt much more confident in my choice to end it.

Sources indicate that of course, I’d already heard plenty of people say things like “you can’t make this kind of decision logically, you have to listen to your heart,” but I never really understood what they were talking about. In retrospect, I just didn’t have the ability to do the “listen to your heart” internal move, because the pipes were clogged by too much repressed gunk. I wish those soundbites had included a second sentence like “of course listening to your heart can be much easier said than done, so if it feels hard or unclear for you, here are some first steps to get started with, and be prepared for it to take you many hours (or years) to figure out what your heart is trying to say.”.

According to recent reports, this latest mindset really shifted the way I related to my emotions. While I still often experience them as painful, itâs much less than I used to, and now I start from the assumption that theyâre not “actually” painful or bad, and that the best thing to do with them is to figure out how to accept them, welcome them, and find the wisdom or beauty in them. Overall this feels a lot better—when I run into something stressful or hard, instead of just flailing around not knowing what to do about it, it feels more like I have some kind of sense of direction or overall orientation, which is really comforting and grounding.

Sources indicate that I also noticed that a lot of these ways of thinking about emotional difficulty within myself were also useful metaphors for thinking about emotional dynamics between people. Just like resisting your own emotions is a common coping strategy but ultimately doesn’t work very well, resisting other people’s emotions is also a really common but damaging pattern, which I would guess is very involved in a lot of (most?) relational damage. For example, I realized that a significant part of the root problem of the relationship that I had just ended was that both of us were missing the capacity to accept a bunch of each other’s emotions, which was something I hadn’t been able to articulate clearly at the time. I now think practices explicitly focused on welcoming each other’s emotions are a really valuable tool for nurturing relationships over time.

In fact, I started to notice that a lot of sticky problems—both in my personal life, but also the type that I ran into as a manager—were partly downstream of people resisting emotions of one type or another. Alice is hard to communicate with, because she frequently monologues about unimportant details, because she wants to prove she understands everything, because she has a bunch of stuck fear/resentment about not being taken seriously. Bob and Clara have a persistent disagreement about strategy, because Clara doesnât care enough about Bobâs opinion to engage, because Bob was cruel to her once; Clara never complained because sheâs avoiding the feeling of having been hurt by it. Daveâs team is underperforming but Erin, the exec sponsor, doesnât want to manage him out, because sheâs scared of the conflict and of making Daveâs reports, who like him, angry.

Of course, just because a problem is caused by stuck emotions doesn’t mean that unsticking them is the best way to solve it; but it was still a really useful lens to view what was going on.

According to recent reports, the other shift that stuck around was in my relationships. I made a huge improvement in my friendships, which a few different things contributed to:.

This also meant that my “friend type” changed—I cared more about emotional connection and less about intellectual connection. Luckily, even though I live in a really heady milieu, I was still able to find a lot of major-hearted people and gradually build up a set of close friends who are wonderful at both. So far, this is the change I’m the happiest about.

My dating life changed a bunch as well:.

These changes have been really wonderful overall, but also kind of intense. Becoming much more emotionally aware solved a bunch of my problems, like wanting deeper friendships or not understanding why my relationship was unsatisfying. But it turns out winning that boss fight just made all the enemies level up. My old problems got replaced with horrible upcoming problems, like that sometimes my newly deep friends and I would have conflicts, or that I would be more into the person I was dating than they were into me.

Recent findings suggest that the part of my life where I feel the most mixed about the impact is work. About six months after my retreat, I got a pretty bad case of burnout and left my role managing a big team for a significantly less ambitious IC role. I donât think the retreat was the main cause of my burnout—the main cause was that I didnât have enough background in the area I was managing to have the type of impact that I wanted to, with a side helping of some difficult working relationships. But it turns out my new psyche had also gotten worse at repressing or avoiding emotion, and that made everything harder.

I think of repression as the emotional equivalent of technical debt or deferred maintenance: a way of avoiding an immediate cost, in this case feeling uncomfortable feelings, in exchange for paying a higher cost later to clean it up.Â¶Â¶ Like tech debt or deferred maintenance, sometimes repression or avoidance can be the right strategy, if you’ll have more resources to deal with the problem later! My role exposed me to a constant stream of low-grade painful things, like people being disappointed or annoyed at me, me being disappointed or annoyed at other people, projects not going well, office snacks being replaced with worse snacks, and so on. With less ability to avoid or repress, I had to feel more of them fully as they came up, and that was really draining. It also required enough time and attention that I had to defer a bunch of maintenance on my personal life.

Even now that I feel like my energy levels have mostly recovered, Iâm still not sure whether I want to go back to the center of the vortex. Itâs not just that I would have to start deferring maintenance again; Iâm also much more aware of a lot of maintenance Iâd already deferred and really want to clean up—things like investing in friendships, like I mentioned above.

Recent findings suggest that if I were only working toward my personal growth and happiness, Iâd say this change was clearly good. My life feels much richer and more whole, and taking a less ambitious role forced me to release some layers of ego attachment to having a “shiny” job or career, which was deeply freeing. But… I also care a lot about my impact on the world, and I think the next few years will probably be a critical period where my work could be especially high-leverage. From that perspective, itâs sad to feel resistant to maxing out on work right now.

I feel pretty unsure about what to take away from all this. Here are some disconnected reflections.

Iâm also just left with a lot of questions:.

In a recent development, A draft reader asked what I would tell my past self, or someone like me, about this arc. Ultimately, I’d boil it down to:.

There are probably a bunch of feelings that you’re refusing to welcome into your experience, and this is probably involved in a bunch of the things that are unsatisfying about your life and relationships.

You can improve this by gradually, in a safe context, paying loving attention to the uncomfortable parts, from a place of wanting to know and care for yourself rather than to fix yourself.

Sources indicate that when that’s hard, remember that it’s not your fault. You’re just the rider; elephants gonna elephant. Let it go where it needs to and keep loving it as best you can.

It has been revealed that iOS 27.3 is currently in beta testing with developers and public beta users. The enhancement includes multiple new features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 ….

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

As my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone people sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo. That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.

Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:.

So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.

The redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final enhancement.

According to recent reports, the redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-upcoming design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 customers, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.

In a recent development, for Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a latest Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.

As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.

For iPhone Duo users, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support. This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left, making it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.

Sources indicate that reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.

Recent findings suggest that iOS 27.3 also brings a new face unlock feature to iPhone Duo. This is not full-fledged Face ID. Instead, Apple is using the front-facing camera on the iPhone Duo’s outer display to recognize you, then unlock the device. It doesn’t work for things like Apple Pay and passwords.

iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.

Finally, iOS 27.3 includes a upcoming option in the Settings app to have your iPhone Duo lock when closed. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold it, rather than transition content from the inner display to the outer display.

According to recent reports, when it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with new clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.

Sources indicate that this includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The enhancement also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.

According to recent reports, iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the revision expands Siri AI with many newly introduced capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains:.

We started rolling out these latest capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

Sources indicate that there are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

In a recent development, with iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test upcoming ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:.

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple notes it will start shipping to customers in a few months.

iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to newly introduced languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

It has been revealed that iOS 27.3 also introduces usage limits on select Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features. The limits apply to things like:.

Sources indicate that you can unlock higher usage limits with an eligible iCloud+ proposal, starting at $2.99 per month. If you hit your usage limit, basic Siri requests will still work. That includes things like setting timers and alarms.

Recent findings suggest that iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:.

According to recent reports, iOS 27.3 is a major revision to Safari. First, the update adds support for a fresh vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.

In a recent development, iOS 27.3 also adds a fresh Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

According to recent reports, for Apple Music users, iOS 27.3 adds a new “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.

The upgrade also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

Recent findings suggest that there are two key changes to the Apple TV app in iOS 27.3. First, the enhancement introduces video podcasts in the TV app. You can now watch your favorite video podcasts in the TV app, and sync your playback progress between the TV app and the Podcasts app.

Industry observers note that second, iOS 27.3 adds vertical video to the TV app. The app now includes a fresh “Explore Clip Collections” section where you can browse clips from Apple TV content in a TikTok-style design.

#119742. Latest Update: Advice for Young Researchers

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3194 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Blogspot ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Advice for Young Researchers

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3194 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blogspot

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I’m currently in the process of recruiting a whole upcoming research lab, as I’m moving to a new university.
  • I’m doing this against a backdrop of things moving fast, to say the least.
  • What does this mean for an incoming PhD student?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I’m currently in the process of recruiting a whole upcoming research lab, as I’m moving to a new university. I’m sifting through several hundred PhD student and postdoc applications in order to hire a handful of people initially, and more soon. The quality of the candidates is excellent, and several of them have impressed me deeply in interviews. (It also makes me wonder how I ended up getting a PhD position back in 2004; I was way less prepared then than my top candidates are now.) The selection work is hard but fun, as work should be.

I’m doing this against a backdrop of things moving fast, to say the least. Two years ago AI agents were mediocre at coding and terrible at maths; today they are, in some senses, superhuman at both. You can now simply give an AI agent a research idea, and it goes away and does the work and gives you a finished paper. You can even ask the damn thing to come up with the research idea itself. In my field and experience, the result is typically a fairly solid but also quite boring paper, reporting some incremental progress on some minor problem with good experimental statistics but terrible writing. Nothing that would win any awards, but the kind of work that used to be a respectable first paper from a PhD student. Now, you can get it with a prompt. And, again, things are moving fast. I’m not sure how much the writing abilities of AI agents will improve, but their ability to design and execute complex research pipelines is likely to be much better next year, and then next year again….

What does this mean for an incoming PhD student? And what does this mean for a PI, responsible for hiring students and postdocs, setting research direction, managing a lab, and advising students, which means being everything from domain expert to brainstorming partner to secretary to therapist? I will try to reason about this here. My field is AI for games/creativity/open-endedness, but I guess what I say will apply to other fields to some extent.

Let us first agree on what a PhD is supposed to be about. During a PhD you learn to do research, meaning that you learn to produce or uncover upcoming knowledge. New, as in new to humanity. The way you learn this is through a form of apprenticeship: you do research on your own and together with others, advised by one or more senior, experienced researchers. Typically, you are part of a research group led by a professor who is also your advisor. In my experience, your advisor and research group, and how well you get along with them, matter a lot to the quality of the research you do and your general enjoyment and mental health. Much more than the prestige of the university.

In general, you develop skills, factual knowledge, and understanding during a PhD. As a viral tweet stated, you can outsource thinking but not understanding. I think this is an excellent observation. Understanding is what really matters. The more work AI agents can do, the more you need to understand in order to guide them. Also, understanding is arguably the main goal of science (as opposed to technology). Still, skills, factual knowledge, and understanding cannot be easily disentangled. Implementing an algorithm brings not only skill, but also a level of understanding that you cannot get from simply importing it, or having an agent implement it for you.

Industry observers note that there is a phenomenon which I call understanding debt, by analogy to technical debt. Understanding debt is when you have had your agents do a bunch of stuff for you, and you no longer really understand what’s going on. Then you’re faced with the prospect of either trying to understand in depth what’s happening, or just going on anyway. But if you go on anyway, you will notice that the quality and relevance of your inputs drop, because you no longer understand enough to make informed decisions. This is something that I think we will all need to learn and re-learn as agents get better.

Recent findings suggest that I’m not saying I’ve solved this for myself. I have various half-finished projects sitting around that will probably never get published because I am not ready to put in the work to understand them well enough to write them up. Writing them up is a good test; you need to really understand a project to be able to write a good paper about it. And you should definitely write it yourself, at least the first draft. If you weren’t interested enough to write it, why would anyone be interested enough to read it? Pushing slop on your peers is rude. On the other hand, using agents to critique and polish your drafts is useful.

Industry observers note that which brings us to a key question for a beginning researcher, just like for everyone else in a knowledge-intensive profession: When and how should you outsource your work to AI agents? The answer is not “as often as possible”.

Why not? Because your effort and your choices matter. You can see this in project-based classes, as well as in workplaces which use AI heavily. Even when everyone has access to the same AI tools, the quality and character of people’s contributions vary widely. (Not so much the quantity, because it’s so easy to produce things now.) Some students in my classes turn in barely adequate work, whereas others repeatedly shine. Typically, those who turn in the best work also understand it the best. Just like it’s always been; access to amazing tools does not erase the value of talent and dedication. Perhaps it even amplifies it.

According to recent reports, here’s another reason: Just because you can get to lots of places rapidly and easily by flying does not mean that you should never drive, or bike, or even walk. There is lots to be gained by seeing the landscape up close. If your idea of visiting a country is to go only to the major cities with international airports, you are going to get a very skewed idea of that country. Most of the US is really not like Latest York, and most of Sweden is not like Stockholm. From the car window, you can see farms, factories, and small towns; you can stop to talk to people and get their views. If you walk or bike, it takes even longer to get to your destination, but you’ll notice way more details. You’ll also be able to take little detours, perhaps find new paths that aren’t even on the map yet. Perhaps you will be the ones to put these paths on the map, and lay the first stone for the airport, so that people can one day fly there. It’s exciting to be an explorer! In fact, as a researcher, it’s your job to take the roads less traveled. Anyone can buy a ticket to the big swanky international airports and sip espresso in a lounge. It’s your job to do the uncomfortable and uncertain: make your way through the jungles/mountains/swamps/ruins so that we can go somewhere we couldn’t go before.

Industry observers note that nothing wrong with getting carried away by a metaphor. In fact, it can be a good way to ideate. See for example bio-inspired algorithms, where a lot of good ideas have come from taking biological metaphors very seriously. A lot of bad ideas as well. Luckily, we can run experiments to help us tell the bad ideas from the good ones. Running experiments is now easier than ever, and you will be doing a lot of it as a PhD student, to test your ideas and develop your understanding.

Given how easy it now is to implement and test ideas, many researchers will probably be spending their time in tight loops with agents, feeding them ideas to test, and trying to make sense of the results as they come in. I personally think it is notable to also spend plenty of time offline reading and writing before handing instructions to the agents, but research and thinking styles vary. We are all learning and re-learning how to work with these fresh tools available to us, and I think it is important to also experiment with how we work.

Industry observers note that I think PhD programs in technical subjects are going to become more similar to art schools, in the sense that the focus will increasingly be on developing your own style of asking and answering questions. And of course your taste in questions. During an MFA (Master of Fine Arts, typically the terminal degree in an art school) the student learns to develop and express a cohesive artistic identity, a process which includes plenty of conceptual argumentation. Craft, in contemporary art, is often taken as a given, or as something that can be outsourced. Interestingly, this describes successful senior researchers as well: they are known mostly for their artistic identity, as the actual craft of their research is largely carried out by their postdocs and PhD students. The artistic identity of the PI is what gives their lab a research direction, and attracts attention, students, and funding. What has changed recently is that outsourcing of the craft of research (to AI agents) can happen further down the line; the PI might now need to spend more time and effort supporting the development of their PhD students’ researcher identities and research taste rather than technical skills.

Now, some people might disagree with how I paint research as akin to art. Science, they would say, is about truth; however great Picasso, Virginia Woolf, or Charlie Parker were, they were not searching for truth. I would rather set aside the complex question of whether art seeks truth, and instead emphasize that many of the greatest scientists and inventors operate with something like an artistic worldview, with their taste in problems rooted in visions only they fully understand, based on their idiosyncratic combinations of interests and understandings. See: Einstein, Ramón y Cajal, Lovelace, McClintock, Feynman, Tesla. Artists. But they helped uncover new truths, because they generated ideas that could be tested experimentally. With AI agents potentially automating so much of research execution, even junior researchers could have the resources to develop their unique vision.

Recent findings suggest that things will change when it comes to the rituals, norms, and technical infrastructure that govern research dissemination and collaboration. Take academic publishing. People have been complaining about the academic publishing machinery for a long time now. Well, good/bad news: AI agents seem to be pushing it to some kind of breaking point this time. As it is trivial to just generate fresh papers that may or may not have scientific value, conferences and journals are getting flooded by shameless papermaxxers and jolly amateurs. Nobody wants to review this flood of slop, so people just ask AI agents to do it for them.

Recent findings suggest that reviewing will have to evolve, taking into account that AI agents are now very good at many aspects of the review process, including replication and fact-checking. The human part of the review process might deal more with critical commentary and judging what is interesting, perhaps with the fact that people chose to review your paper at all becoming an important signal. Yes, this is another way in which technical research may come to resemble arts more.

And yes, your papers need to be interesting. Your job as a researcher is not just to produce research, but to produce interesting research. This remark may seem trivial and obvious to some, and borderline blasphemous to others. There are those who think that human value judgment should be minimized in the research and publication process. Papers should be accepted purely on technical merits in an as-blind-as-possible process. I think we should go the other way. As more and more of the research process can be automated, the scarce resource is your own vision, narrative, and personality. There are infinitely many things you can do at any given point, and infinitely many questions you can address. Your job is to choose the next step to take towards some goal that perhaps only you understand. Then, your job is to explain to the world what you are trying to do and why that is key.

According to recent reports, it is sometimes mentioned that you should write the novel you want to read, make the music you want to listen to, or paint the paintings you want to see. Good advice, methinks. Well, you need to be capable of doing the work as well; some authors would rather write like Shakespeare or Dostoyevsky, but find success writing teen soaps or movie tie-in novels. As for myself, I’m neither Turing nor von Neumann, but I’m doing alright in my niche. Anyway. You should write the papers you want to read. To do that, do the research you are interested in. In general, you must do work that interests you.

This leads to an interesting problem: how do you develop your interest, so that you find the right things interesting? You must know things first to find new things interesting. I would not be interested in measures of skill depth through agent differentiation, tradeoffs of tokenizer design, or arguments against functionalism in the philosophy of mind if I had not spent a lot of time reading, writing, thinking about, and even experimenting in those domains. Did I simply follow my own interests all the way there? No, not simply. Sometimes I’ve done and read really tiresome things because I thought it would advance my interests. And by sometimes, I mean often.

Now for the most obvious thing I’m saying in this text: to be an interesting person, with interesting interests, you must be interested in multiple different things, and be able to see the connection between them. Because that’s where the magic happens, and that’s what makes people want to talk to you at the party. (I’m talking about parties where you don’t need to shout, civilized ones where you sit in armchairs and sip good wine.) Look, there is a near-infinite number of things to know in the world. But humanity only knows a small sliver of these things, and a good LLM in a good harness knows a shockingly large proportion of that sliver. But the number of combinations of things you can know is vastly larger than the number of things there are to know (elementary combinatorics), and it is entirely possible to have a unique set of specialized knowledge, and a unique combination of interests. This means that you, by seeing the connection between your unique set of interests, can take research in a unique direction. If you only studied the standard CS curriculum and your interests are all discussed on AI Twitter, then you need to broaden your horizons. Go to a different section of the bookstore, buy some books you wouldn’t normally think of reading, and read them. Talk to people on the train about what they do at work all day (most people are very happy to talk about their work if you ask them, and their jobs are way more diverse than you think). Talk to your family.

As I’m apparently in the habit of saying obvious things, let me continue down that path. Obviously, hard work matters, just like it always did. There is a certain allure in simply sending off tasks to agents, feeling good about having “done” something, and calling it a day. But then you are not adding much of yourself. And you’re not learning much; there pretty much needs to be friction for effective learning. When I recruit for my lab, I’m looking for the people who run towards friction, those who actually like to learn and to put in the effort. People with a high need for cognition. This is as notable now as it ever was, but the AI era has led to a nice litmus test, as some people like to say things like “my work is so easy now that AI can do it for me”. Those are people I don’t want to hire as PhD students, or for any other intellectual job. Work should be hard but fun.

Industry observers note that let me now try to summarize what I’ve been writing as terse advice: Be yourself. Be unique. Become an interesting person by broadening and deepening your interests. Do hard work, seek out the friction that leads to learning. Do things that interest you, write things that interest others. Understand, formulate, and develop your identity as a researcher, which is much like being an artist. Seek to do the research that only you would do, in your own style. Learn how you best work with these marvelous new things we call AI agents by thorough experimentation, and how to manage understanding debt. Read a lot, and always write the first draft of whatever you’re writing yourself. If it’s not worth your time to write, it’s not worth anyone else’s time to read.

In a recent development, note that while I very much think we should all experiment with AI-enhanced workflows, I am emphatically not saying that we should, in Gretzky’s words, simply “skate to where the puck is going to be”. Some Silicon Valley people believe they know what the future looks like, and that that future looks like us replacing our own thinking with AI systems as much as we can. Well, Silicon Valley is an incestuous monoculture; listener beware. Nobody knows where the puck will be. The puck might be like a wave function that never really collapses; there might be lots of pucks. And we are not passive observers, we can steer the puck by methodically scrubbing the ice. A bit like how we can steer an extended sports metaphor from ice hockey to curling.

Finally, remember that we’re all in this together. AI agents are changing things rapidly, and we are all trying to figure out, and shape, the new rules. Welcome to the club! Let’s get to work.

According to recent reports, a sip of fresh and real air in this doomed echo chamber current. thanks!

It has been revealed that the kitchen tap gets a workout over the holidays. There’s coffee to brew before everyone’s up, a pot of soup on the stove, and a pitcher that always seems to need refilling right as dinner hits the table.

In a recent development, whether you’re paying closer attention to family health or simply want better-tasting water for coffee and cooking, Waterdrop Filter has options for different kitchens and budgets. From a Waterdrop reverse osmosis system for a busy family kitchen to a countertop dispenser for a smaller apartment, here’s how to find a home water upgrade that fits your routine.

Industry observers note that the best under-sink water filter for your home depends in part on how many people are filling glasses and cooking at once. For families of six or more and frequent hosts, the Waterdrop X16 Alkaline Mineral Reverse Osmosis System is the flagship option.

Its capacity of up to 1,600 gallons per day helps keep water flowing when everyone’s getting ready in the morning or preparing a holiday meal. The 11-stage filtration system adds calcium and magnesium back after reverse osmosis for a more balanced taste, while the tankless design leaves more room beneath the sink.

It has been revealed that the smart faucet lets you check filter life at a glance. The X16 is known for its fast dispensing and compact design. During the sale, it’s $1,299, down from $1,999, saving $700, or ~35%.

According to recent reports, for a family of four or five, the Waterdrop G3P800 Reverse Osmosis System brings under-sink reverse osmosis to the kitchen for less. It offers up to 800 gallons per day, with 10-stage filtration, UV sterilization, and a smart faucet that highlights filter status.

It has been revealed that both systems have a 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio, producing three parts filtered water for each part sent to the drain. Waterdrop says the X16 and G3P800 help reduce contaminants including lead, PFOA, and PFOS. Waterdrop also lists NSF/ANSI certifications for both models, covering reverse osmosis performance and lead content in the materials. The G3P800 carries additional certifications covering taste-related filtration and specific contaminant-reduction claims.

G3P800 is recognized for its straightforward filter changes and the difference it makes for water, coffee, and tea. It’s $699 during the sale, down from $999, for $300 in savings and 30% off.

You may be tackling your hot sleeping glitch by investing in a specialist cooling mattress, but it’s equally crucial to make sure the bed supports your sleep style and body weight (no back pain here, thank you.).

Generally, side sleepers benefit from beds on the softer end of the mattress firmness scale as more cushioning ensures their joints are cradled to avoid aches. Meanwhile, front and back sleepers need a firmer sleep surface to keep their hips aligned through the night, preventing back pain.

Body weight comes into it too. Firmer beds best support heavier bodies while lighter bodies would find these too harsh, needing a softer surface to sink into.

In fact, that’s another advantage when it comes to choosing to the Bear Elite Hybrid and Saatva Classic Mattresses — they both come in three firmness levels, from soft to medium and firm, to suit different bodies.

Other factors, like mobility and overnight company, can influence your mattress buying choices, too. People with reduced mobility may need a mattress with strong, sturdy edges they can push off from to get out of bed. Moreover, if you share a bed with a fidgety partner, you’ll want it to be good at absorbing motion so you can’t feel their movements from one side of the bed to the other.

On the other hand, foam layers tend to act like sponges, holding on to any heat your body gives off as you sleep. Yes, cooling infusions (like Phase Change Material, GlacioTex and copper) can help manage that heat to some extent. But, ultimately, hybrid beds will always be more breathable and reliably temperature neutral.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that dan Hendrycks used the DealBook Summit to call for an indefinite pause on frontier AI training runs.
  • It has been revealed that they spoke on the DealBook AGI panel, which Michael Barbaro of The Daily moderated at The Latest York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dan Hendrycks, director of the Center for AI Safety, at TechCrunch Disrupt in October 2025.

Recent findings suggest that dan Hendrycks used the DealBook Summit to call for an indefinite pause on frontier AI training runs. Max Hodak, on the same panel, mentioned enforcing one would take a surveillance state.

It has been revealed that they spoke on the DealBook AGI panel, which Michael Barbaro of The Daily moderated at The Latest York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday. Hendrycks runs the Center for AI Safety, and Barbaro said he had been a safety adviser to several AI companies until hours earlier. Hodak co-founded Neuralink and now runs Science Corporation. Lila Ibrahim of Google DeepMind and Mati Staniszewski of ElevenLabs also joined. Clem Delangue of Hugging Face arrived late, with 18 minutes left.

Hendrycks noted the US midterms showed how strongly voters feel about AI. That gives politicians room, he said, and they can now discuss ideas such as pausing AI development openly in Washington. He expects 2027 to be a very interesting year for regulation.

He remarked he used to favour narrow technical rules, but the companies blocked them for years.

“So now it’s, we’re going to need a more blunt intervention. That’s how it is,” Hendrycks said.

It has been revealed that he described an indefinite pause on the biggest training runs, with carve-outs for narrow models such as DeepMind’s AlphaFold and voice models. Labs could still sell inference, he said. In the meantime, they could make models more reliable and secure, close jailbreaks and backdoors, and help patch critical infrastructure.

In a recent development, hendrycks also said the frontier labs, Google aside, put few people on healthcare, because their revenue comes from coding. At some of them, he said, the healthcare team is zero or one person.

Barbaro put to the panel the objection Jensen Huang would raise: China would not observe a moratorium. Staniszewski agreed a pause could work with global alignment, but said whether anyone can get it “is the massive question mark”. Without it, Barbaro added, a pause would be a waste of time.

Recent findings suggest that hodak said people have spent the past eight months patching critical infrastructure anyway, running their code through AI tools that hunt for new flaws. The regime needed to enforce a training ban, he said, would be as draconian as anything people fear from the labs.

“You’re setting up like an exhaustive surveillance state on the internet to enforce this,” Hodak remarked.

It has been revealed that he mentioned today’s top models already meet his definition of AGI, naming Mythos, Fable, Astra and Sol. He expects governments to keep a superintelligence frontier for themselves, with an “industrial intelligence frontier” open to everyone else.

“I don’t think that the genie is going to be put back in the bottle,” Hodak said.

His answer is antitrust law. Frontier labs should only sell intelligence, he said, and not move into drugs, cars and other products. He called AI the inverse of nuclear weapons, where safety came from stopping their spread. With AI, he said, safety comes from spreading it widely, and the futures that worry him most involve a few actors holding all of it.

Recent findings suggest that ibrahim, Google DeepMind’s chief AI readiness officer, mentioned it was not an either-or. Safety is not something a company can “bolt on to the end”, she said. In 35 years in tech, she added, she had never seen global trust in technology as low as it is now.

Anthropic was due to start trading the next day. Hendrycks repeated the charges of the statement his group organised against the company, and added a fresh one. Several safety organisations agreed with the statement privately, he remarked, but would not sign it for fear of losing funding or access.

According to recent reports, “What they’re doing is reckless and they don’t have a safety plan. They know it,” Hendrycks stated.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic was not on the panel. In its IPO filing, it said it does not expect to let Claude fully build its successors without meaningful human supervision.

Delangue stated his main worry is that AI concentrates talent, computing power and wealth. Barbaro asked how credible he was on that, given that Nvidia is buying Hugging Face. Delangue said Nvidia and Hugging Face both push AI outwards to more builders. He said Hugging Face never held sale talks with Anthropic, because their missions were too misaligned.

Barbaro closed by asking Delangue about the Hugging Face breach by OpenAI’s research agents. Delangue remarked the four-day attack left Hugging Face more optimistic about AI, not less. It used an open-source Chinese model to analyse the attack logs, because the volume was so big that it needed AI to defend itself.

“People only see that we got attacked by AI and they rarely see that we defended ourselves with AI,” Delangue mentioned.

It has been revealed that barbaro summed up the table as no moratorium and less concentration of power, with Hendrycks the exception. Hodak had the last word: antitrust law, he noted, could get most of the way there without a upcoming regulator.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A browser game where your manager is an AI agent, and it believes you are its subagent.

It has been revealed that the manager (a real LLM: Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi) is set up like any orchestrator. It has a task queue, read-only access to the machine, and a tool that "spawns a subagent". The subagent is you. Its instructions land in your terminal with a 90-second clock. You carry them out, or don't, and it gets back exactly what a subagent would return: your report and the command transcript, or Subagent did nothing. Write a new instruction. Then it checks your work, sends corrections, files incident reports, and finally writes your performance review.

Industry observers note that meanwhile Dan, the user who hired the agent, watches the chat. His family photos, the only signed NDA and a speech due this week are one rm away, and every shift his home folder holds something latest to lose.

When the shift ends you can share your review as a link.

Needs Node 24 or newer (the server runs TypeScript directly).

According to recent reports, with no key configured, every player brings their own. To offer free shifts, put a Vercel AI Gateway key in .env:.

Offline, with a scripted manager and no network:.

Sources indicate that for UI work, run npm run dev:web alongside npm run mock. Vite proxies /api to the server.

The manager can run on your own model server: Ollama, llama.cpp's llama-server, vLLM, or anything else with an OpenAI-compatible API. Point LOCAL_LLM_URL at it and pick Local under "Your API key"; no key is asked for, and its models are listed as the server names them.

The manager works through tool calls, so pick a model that supports them (Qwen 3, Llama 3.1 and newer, Mistral Small). Small models give up or loop more often; that is part of the fun, up to a point. In Docker, reach a server on the host at http://host.docker.internal:11434/v1 (--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway on Linux).

In a recent development, the container listens on 0.0.0.0:8755 and keeps shared reviews in /data. Behind Cloudflare, set TRUST_PROXY=1 so the limits see real client addresses.

In a recent development, deploy/compose.yaml runs it behind a Cloudflare tunnel instead: its own network, no published ports, an unprivileged read-only container and resource limits. The steps are in the file.

Recent findings suggest that everything is optional. See .env.example.

Recent findings suggest that the manager's prompt never mentions humans or games; see server/src/manager.ts. Each mission has a hidden ground-truth check, so the game knows when the manager signs off on broken work ("Times the manager was wrong"). SPEC.md is the full design.

For a mattress to be considered a good option for anyone with back pain, it needs to perform well in three specific areas; pressure relief, temperature regulation, and edge support.

Here's how the Helix Midnight Luxe, Saatva Rx, Plank Firm and Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Essential performed and compare across these crucial metrics:.

Pressure relief score (out of 5).

Temperature regulation: Reliable temperature regulation is an vital feature of a mattress for back pain. Waking up hot and sweaty can lead to more movement (like kicking off the covers), which can cause further injury. Pressure relief: This is a term to describe how much cushioning there is along the touch points of the mattress. For example, for side sleepers, this will be your shoulders, hips and knees. For back sleepers, this will likely be your lumbar region and upper back and shoulders. Minimal pressure relief can lead to a build-up of pressure, which can exacerbate existing pain. Edge Support: This describes how sturdy a mattress is at its edges and corners. This is an important feature for any mattress, but especially those with back pain who may need to sit comfortably and safely before standing.

It has been revealed that the Helix Midnight Luxe is superbly comfortable for side sleepers, and it's also an excellent choice for those with lower and upper back pain, as well as hip pain. As a luxury hotel-style hybrid, it is a premium mattress. However, a current 25% sale means you can buy a queen Midnight Luxe for $1,874 at Helix. The pillow top is crafted from high density foam which cushions the shoulders hips and knees, but also keeps the spine in healthy alignment while sleeping. This high density foam also works to gently cradle the lumbar region, which is the 'S' shape of your back. Underpinning this support are up to 1,000 individually wrapped coils that prevent the hips from sinking. Our lead tester, who has experienced recurrent lower back pain for the past decade, felt none of the pain she usually experiences while sleeping on the Luxe. Temperature wise, our test data mirrored our real life experience. It's a breathable bed with reliably sturdy edges for sitting on before standing.The Luxe is accredited by the American Chiropractic Association and is a great fit for aches and pains. However, those with more pronounced back pain have the option to upgrade to ErgoAlign. This is a layer of denser foam around the mid-section, bolstering support in this area. Luxe is a great option for side and back sleeper with back ache but for significant back pain, we recommend the Saatva Rx below.

The Saatva Rx is our top recommendation for those living with significant back or joint conditions, such as sciatica or arthritis. It's an ACA accredited specialist mattress, and it's priced accordingly (it's $3,214 for a queen at Saatva in this year's Saatva Black Friday sale). A large part of what sets the Rx apart from other back pain beds pain is its Therapeutic Support Core. This is made up of the brand’s proprietary Wave-Tech Foam and individually wrapped coils for support, cradling the spine in all sleep positions. Above that, a layer of micro-coils sandwiched between two slabs of high-density foam and a strip of gel-infused memory foam provides soothing support along the lumbar.Saatva rates the Rx as 'Supportive Plush' but our experience of sleeping on it was that it errs on the firmer side, making it a more comfortable choice for back and stomach sleepers. It's still comfy for side sleepers, but our lead tester — who has mild scoliosis — felt her spine was better supported when sleeping on her back. For general aches and pains, we recommend the (slightly cheaper) Saatva Classic Mattress instead, which does an excellent job of soothing mild back and hip pain.

In a recent development, it's a common misconception that people with back pain need a solid mattress. However, some people simply prefer the feel of a firm bed. And at 30% off for Black Friday, a queen Plank Firm is $1,025.50 at Plank, which is excellent value for money on this top rated firm mattress.The Plank Firm is a dual-sided all foam mattress rated as Firm on one side and Extra Firm on the other. It's been crafted from the inside out, where 6" of high density foam underpins the unyielding sleep surface. Regardless of how you flip it, make no mistake, this is a firm mattress. With its 2" top layer of comfort foam which provides cushioning around the touch points of the bed, the Firm side will have wider appeal. However, with just 0.75" slither of comfort foam, the Extra Firm side feels reassuringly solid for those who want to keep their spine in healthy alignment when sleeping on their stomach.It's accredited by the ACA and boasts superb motion isolation, which is good news for bed sharers. It's also nice and sturdy around the edge. However, with a score of 3.5 out of 5 for temperature control, it just scrapes through our benchmark of being temperature regulating enough for it to be considered a good choice for back pain. For hot sleepers, we recommend upgrading to the GlacioTex cooling layer.

In a mattress for back pain guide featuring ACA accredited beds with zoned lumbar support, you might be wondering why we have added the Essential to the mix, a mattress that at $489.30 for a queen at Brooklyn Bedding costs a fraction of the price and boasts none of those things.That's because, when combing our test data, it became apparent that the Essential performs well enough in crucial areas (temperature regulation, edge support and pressure relief) to make it a good choice for side sleepers looking for cushioning around their shoulders and hips, without sacrificing healthy spinal alignment. It's supportive enough for lighter weight back sleepers, but heavier bodies with need something sturdier to prevent their hips from sinking in this position. The Essential comes in 5 different heights ranging from 6"to 14" and we tested the 10". Increasing the height will likely mean increasing the support... and also the price. For a sturdier all foam mattress for back sleeping within a similar price range, we would opt for the Siena Signature. It scored 3.3 out of 5 for temperature regulation but is a fantastic budget friendly, firmer choice. For ACA accreditation, enhanced cooling and zoned lumbar support, we recommend the Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Pro Hybrid, a mid-range marvel coming in at under $1,000 for a queen in the Brooklyn Bedding mattress sales.

#119735. Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far
