Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (953 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that “It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple.
  • Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….
  • Macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that “It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple. Interestingly, it appears to have been coined by the tech giant’s customers and then used by reviewers before it was later picked up by Steve Jobs.

Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….

Macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing. It was subsequently used by a number of reviewers. The earliest example I can find of Steve Jobs adopting it was in 1999, when discussing the rollout of FireWire to the Mac in the PowerMac G3.

According to recent reports, it’s hot-pluggable. You don’t have to turn your computer off to connect and disconnect peripherals, you can just plug them right in. Again, the drivers are dynamically loaded. There are no terminators and there are no switches. It just works.

(If you have a link to any earlier example, please do let me know in the comments.).

Industry observers note that I’m a big fan of the philosophy. Most of the time, people should just be able to get on with the tasks they want to execute without having to worry about the technology. The tech that makes it all possible should sit there quietly in the background.

However, there are cases where I think Apple takes this approach a little too far, and where tech-savvy consumers at least would like a little more transparency and control.

AirPods firmware updates are a good example. Back in September, there was quite a significant revision in the form of custom EQ. It’s a rather basic version, but still a feature many had wanted for a long time. Instead of being able to manually trigger the update, customers had to wait until it “just worked.”.

It has been revealed that apple’s support document has a how-to guide that is essentially an outline of the conditions required to permit an enhancement, and an instruction to simply wait until it happens. Which you will only know by repeatedly checking.

Make sure your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Connect your charging case to a power source. Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to be updated. Check the firmware version again.

In a recent development, another example, and one I’ve complained about before, is that there is no way to manually trigger an iCloud document sync, nor any progress indicator when it does finally happen. In the best of cases, it takes seconds; in the worst, many hours. And again, the only way to find out is to repeatedly check.

Sources indicate that it’s the same story when shooting a video on your iPhone. Will it still be there an hour later, available to instantly edit and view? Maybe, or maybe it will have been offloaded to the cloud, requiring it to be downloaded before you can do anything with it – while a video you shot months earlier is still stored locally on the device! You can, of course, switch off optimization altogether, but if you choose to use it, you get no control over it. I want a setting that allows me to do things like specify local retention of all photos and videos taken within the past fortnight.

In a recent development, will that video be available in the Mac Photos app when you check half an hour later? Maybe, maybe not. You can click the Sync Now button as many times as you like, and it will apparently have no effect, claiming it’s up to date despite the video being entirely absent. It will be there when it’s there.

Industry observers note that once it is in the Photos app on your Mac, it’s a similar story when exporting it to a folder. You can drag and drop the video into the folder, and this time you are manually triggering the transfer (yay!), but there will be absolutely no visual indication that it is in progress. No grayed-out icon, no progress bar, nothing. So far as the user interface is concerned, it appears that your drag and drop had no effect – until the video file finally appears.

Sources indicate that I think with all of these things and more, Apple needs to offer options. Yes, most non-tech users may be perfectly happy to just wait until things happen, but there ought to be a standard way to trigger things that currently happen in their own sweet time, as well as progress indicators and confirmation that a process is complete.

In a recent development, is this an ecosystem-wide improvement you’d like to see? Please share your thoughts in the comments and add any frustrating examples of your own.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anduril founder Palmer Luckey speaks at Space Systems Command, Los Angeles Air Force Base, El Segundo, 6 August 2026.
  • Palmer Luckey indicates the US government will not let Ukraine use Starshield, because it fears Russia would destroy it.
  • “The US government isn’t even willing to stand up for Ukraine because they’re afraid of losing their constellation,” Luckey stated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anduril founder Palmer Luckey speaks at Space Systems Command, Los Angeles Air Force Base, El Segundo, 6 August 2026.

Palmer Luckey indicates the US government will not let Ukraine use Starshield, because it fears Russia would destroy it. Starshield is the Pentagon’s military satellite network, and SpaceX helps run it. The Anduril founder made the case to Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday.

“The US government isn’t even willing to stand up for Ukraine because they’re afraid of losing their constellation,” Luckey stated.

He was defending Elon Musk, who spoke later that day and accused Zelenskyy of lying about Starshield speed limits. Luckey said he likes Musk personally, so people should take his view “with a pound of salt”.

Industry observers note that his argument ran like this. Russia has hinted that it could destroy the civilian Starlink network if Ukraine keeps using it for attacks. The same satellites that cover Ukraine also orbit over the US. So Musk should not have to risk his whole network when Washington will not risk its own, Luckey said.

“Nobody in the West actually wants Ukraine to win. They just want them to not lose for as long as possible, which is a bizarre and absurd warfighting position,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that luckey stated he fully supports Ukraine, and that Anduril has worked there since the second day of the war. Who America sells weapons to is not his call, he added.

“I’m a dog on a chain and I need to be kept that way,” Luckey said.

Recent findings suggest that luckey co-leads Project Meridian, the Pentagon’s 120-day study of future war, with Musk and Newt Gingrich. He said it looks at what war could look like in 2050, and that the MITRE Corporation runs it. The group met at Cheyenne Mountain the day before. It agreed to focus on ideas that have no champion in the Pentagon.

One example is weather control, he said, such as changing where rain falls at sea so forces get a clearer view of targets. He also took credit for pushing the Trump administration to rename the Defense Department the Department of War.

It has been revealed that sorkin read him a criticism from Wes Bryant, who until last year ran the Pentagon’s assessment of civilian harm. Bryant called Meridian a sign of oligarchy in government. Luckey noted more than 20 people sit on it, including retired generals and admirals. Nobody attacked Eric Schmidt for joining the Defense Innovation Board under Joe Biden, he said, and the report will be public.

Recent findings suggest that luckey wants the US to resume nuclear testing, mainly to see what an electromagnetic pulse does to modern electronics. The models used today were built for transistors thousands of times larger than those in a phone, he stated. He is not confident his own systems would survive, even when built to the hardening rules.

“They were designed for the type of cell phone that Abraham Lincoln would have used,” he noted.

Industry observers note that he said no AI model can be controlled, because every major model has been jailbroken within months. Data centres can still be shut off, he added. The AI in weapons is a different technology from chatbots, he argued, and more reliable than the older seekers it replaces.

“I am way more afraid of the civilian collateral side for dumb weapons than I am for smart weapons,” Luckey stated.

Recent findings suggest that some companies have used chatbots for targeting and made mistakes, he remarked, without naming them. China wants Jensen Huang out of Nvidia, he said, so he wants him back. Luckey still opposes selling chips to China.

Luckey also defended public executions. The state should rarely use the death penalty, he noted. When it does, it should do so in public and without medical cover, so people can judge whether it got it right.

It has been revealed that “Executions should be brutal. They should be violent,” he remarked.

In a recent development, he closed on his 2017 firing from Facebook, after he gave $9,000 to a pro-Trump group. He blames former Oculus colleagues, not Mark Zuckerberg, and now works with Meta on a combat headset for the US Army.

“It’s probably better for everybody that I got fired, but I have not let it go,” Luckey said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’ve used Apple’s Calendar app for years, and there’s an elegant simplicity to it. But one key area the app has long lagged behind competitors is event creation.

When you need to create a latest event, the Calendar app historically has required manually filling in various fields for the title, date, time, invitees, etc. By contrast, the excellent third-party app Fantastical lets you type in natural language and it automatically fills in relevant parameters based on what you type.

In iOS 27, Apple finally introduces its own natural language input for Calendar events. You can type out your event details and certain recognized parameters will be used to automatically fill in the detail fields.

While the feature still isn’t on par with what Fantastical offers, since it doesn’t support as many data points as the third-party alternative, it’s very much a step in the right direction.

Recent findings suggest that apple has always pitched Siri as being like a personal assistant. As such, calendar-related tasks should have been Siri’s strong suit. But until iOS 27, you couldn’t actually manage your calendar very well using Siri.

With Siri AI, that’s changed in a big way. Now, you can do things like:.

Recent findings suggest that one of my favorite personal examples is from this summer when the NFL schedule was released. I asked Siri to find the Dallas Cowboys schedule and add every game to my calendar, and it pulled this off with ease.

Siri is so much better than before at assisting with your calendar, and iOS 27.3 will bring even more capabilities soon.

What are your favorite iOS 27 Apple Calendar upgrades? Let us know in the comments.

#119728. FT, NYT tie Alice Huang’s chip network to gaming tycoons and PLA suppliers

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (814 w)

Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

FT, NYT tie Alice Huang’s chip network to gaming tycoons and PLA suppliers

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia’s headquarters on San Tomas Expressway in Santa Clara, California.
  • Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive at the centre of the Nvidia scandal, had links to gaming tycoons, hundreds of shell companies and an alleged Cambodian criminal group, the Financial Times reported on Saturday.
  • It has been revealed that TNW has not independently verified either report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia’s headquarters on San Tomas Expressway in Santa Clara, California.

Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive at the centre of the Nvidia scandal, had links to gaming tycoons, hundreds of shell companies and an alleged Cambodian criminal group, the Financial Times reported on Saturday. Together they formed a network that supplied Nvidia chips to China. A day earlier, The New York Times tied companies linked to her family to suppliers of China’s military.

It has been revealed that TNW has not independently verified either report. US officials suspect Huang of working for Chinese intelligence, the Times first reported in October, describing a Chinese spy plot. Beijing calls the claim a smear. Jensen Huang quit as Nvidia’s chief executive on 12 November after admitting an affair with her. They are not related.

Industry observers note that the FT’s Zijing Wu and Haohsiang Ko traced the Alice Huang chip network through hundreds of filings and more than a dozen sources. Its companies made billions moving Nvidia chips into China, not necessarily aware of the full picture, the paper reported.

It started with Inspur, one of Nvidia’s largest server partners in China. The US put Inspur on its entity list in March 2023, but not its part-owned US unit. Renamed Aivres, that unit kept trading with Nvidia. Inside Nvidia there were questions over whether it should count as a partner, a person with direct knowledge told the FT. Nvidia concluded that it met all compliance and export control rules.

Some of Inspur’s Chinese clients then turned to Century Huatong, an online gaming group turned data centre investor. The answer, people familiar with the plan said, was an offshore shell branded as a “neocloud”. That shell became Megaspeed, with Huang as its trusted public face.

Kang Wei, whom the FT calls her husband and the Times her business partner, was an early investor in Century Huatong, filings show. Megaspeed grew out of the Singapore arm of 7Road, a gaming firm that Huang and Century Huatong both backed. Its Malaysian unit, Speedmatrix, declared about $4.6bn of imports from Aivres in the year to December 2025. The FT cites ImportGenius trade data.

Industry observers note that the last step was smuggling the chips into China. Hu Xiaowei filled at least part of that role, people familiar with the matter told the FT. US authorities call Hu the “second-in-command” at Prince Group. The US Treasury has named the group a transnational criminal organisation. Hu was arrested in Japan this summer.

In a recent development, A spokesperson for the Prince group of companies said Hu never worked for the business and called the US allegations unsupported. The FT could not reach Hu.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia said it put Megaspeed and a subsidiary on its block list in 2025 and has also restricted sales to Aivres. Megaspeed has said it runs a lawful business, and that Huang left in August 2025. Tencent, which owns 10.1% of Century Huatong, said it knew nothing of the activities. The FT found no evidence that Tencent or Alibaba took part.

The Times reviewed a confidential analysis by Strider Technologies, an intelligence firm staffed by former intelligence officers. About $3.6bn of Chinese state money flowed through companies tied to Huang’s family or associates, it found. The money funded projects including data centres with Nvidia chips. The Times noted it confirmed many of the ties itself.

Most links are indirect, the Times mentioned, and it is unclear whether the military used any of the computing power. The paper had already reported that Megaspeed’s backer Alibaba co-founded a military-linked lab.

“Follow the money and, too often, you find the P.L.A. at the end of it,” Strider’s chief executive, Greg Levesque, told the Times.

Industry observers note that both papers point to Century Litong, a Shanghai firm founded by Century Longteng. The FT says Longteng was a venture between Century Huatong and a vehicle Huang controlled with her sister. The Times names the sister’s firm.

Century Litong was a key distributor of smuggled Nvidia chips in China, people with knowledge of the deals told the FT. The Information first reported its role. Its owner, Jiangsu Lettall Electronic, also controls a maker of Chinese radar and missile parts, the Times reported.

It has been revealed that nvidia sought permission to sell more than 40,000 H200s to Century Litong’s Hong Kong unit, licence files released on Thursday by a House committee show. An Nvidia spokesman told the Times that, despite receiving some licences, it had already stopped shipping H200s to China, and had not and would not ship to that firm. Century Litong notes it has no dealings with Huang. Nvidia’s shares, meanwhile, have had their worst run since 2008.

From value creation to value extraction.

By Tim O’Reilly November 20, 2026 • 32 minute read.

On October 16, 2026, I delivered the second Annual Margaret Levi Lecture in Political Economy  in conjunction with the AI and History conference at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. This is my original lecture as written, which incorporates material from many pieces I’ve written over the years. As delivered, I departed significantly from the script, as you can see from the embedded video below or the transcript that you can see at the link above.

It has been revealed that it’s an honor to give a lecture in Margaret Levi’s name. I’ve been asked to reflect on the changes in the political economy of Silicon Valley throughout my 40-plus year career in and about it, and I can’t imagine a better framing for my remarks than Margaret’s vision.

According to recent reports, margaret understood that advances in our ability to work together are essential to a better future. Cooperation is the human superpower. She also asks what happens when the systems of cooperation we have constructed over time stop holding up their end of the bargain.

Sources indicate that that is very much the question that Silicon Valley is facing today. An industry that pioneered advances in collective intelligence at scale used to engender love from its customers because of the way it solved new problems in their lives. It now too often inspires fear and loathing. How did things go so wrong?

Sources indicate that but let me start with my own history. I started my tech giant more than 40 years ago with a $500 initial investment. We took in no venture capital, and we built a business that now generates hundreds of millions of dollars in profitable annual revenue, funded by customers who love our products and pay us for them. We got there the slow way, through steady organic growth. That is quite anathema to the rush to the top of whatever appears to be the latest hill that seems to characterize Silicon Valley today. Even when climbing that hill traps a company at a local maximum, the hope is to get to payday before the industry moves on to the next hill.

Sources indicate that my original corporate goal was stated as simply “Interesting work for interesting people.” That evolved into two principles: “Change the world by spreading the knowledge of innovators,” and “Create more value than you capture.” Those principles shaped not only my tech giant but what I expected the internet to be. When we launched GNN, the Global Network Navigator, in 1993, it was the first web portal and the first ad-supported site on the World Wide Web, and for two years it was the place people went to find other sites. What we built was a machine for pointing you at the best of what other people had made, and then getting out of your way.

Even our idea of advertising was not what you think of today. It was inspired by direct mail advertising, where you’d read articles in a print magazine or look at accompanying ads, and then you’d call an 800 number or circle a number on a “bingo card” that you’d send in to the publisher so that the advertiser could send you a brochure. I realized that the web would be a good replacement for that awkward system, that every organization ought to have its own website that provided more information about its products and services. What we invented was not the “grab your attention” kind of advertising. It was all about utility, and sharing information that customers really wanted and needed. In short, it was the commercial web, which no one any longer thinks of as advertising, even though it is the most durable and useful kind.

In a recent development, the commercial web was only a small part of what the web became. The web was the playground of amateurs, not entrepreneurs. It was a marvelous collective work of human imagination, creativity, sharing, and ultimately (though that became toxic only later), competition for attention. Our hand-curated catalog of the best websites was soon surpassed by algorithmic solutions like those provided by Google. The amount of content produced was far larger than purely human curation could manage. It was an early example of what Richard Sutton was later to call “the bitter lesson” in his analysis of AI training.

In my 2005 essay “What Is Web 2.0?” I described how the companies that survived the dotcom bust had all, in one way or another, figured out how to help people navigate the resulting information explosion at scale. As Herbert Simon noted in 1971, an abundance of information leads to a scarcity of attention. In the face of increasing information abundance, he predicted that we would use machines to help us better allocate our time and attention. And so it has transpired: Information has become so abundant that it defies manual curation. Instead, powerful, proprietary algorithmic systems use the data they collect to match users with the answers, news, entertainment, products, applications, and services they seek. Today’s AI is in many ways a continuation of this arc.

Recent findings suggest that I called this “harnessing collective intelligence.” All of it was, in economic terms, a set of remarkable advances in networked, data-enabled market coordination. It felt like a public good even when it was privately owned.

Hal Varian, formerly Google’s chief economist, once told me that only about 6% of Google search result pages carry any advertising or are otherwise monetized by Google. The other 94% were served up by search in a glorious demonstration of abundance, the surplus of value created over value captured. And while many of the pages themselves were commercial, even more were the product of the joyful exuberance of humanity, people creating and sharing for the joy of it. Google’s algorithm matched that creation to the people who wanted it, with no price involved anywhere in the transaction. Forty thousand times a second, Google’s organic search algorithms were performing the coordination that twentieth-century economists thought could only be done by self-interested actors haggling over prices. And for Google’s first decade and a half, the priced market of advertising ran alongside organic search as a sidecar, not the engine.

That’s the Silicon Valley I signed up for. Some of this is nostalgia. The early web had plenty wrong with it, its share of greedy hustlers and hypesters. But value creation for both owners and suppliers was the winning strategy. Companies won by solving real problems for their customers. Investors won when the tech giant delivered on their promises. Unfortunately, that didn’t last.

Google, a company once known for “Don’t be evil,” now faces the same surveillance-capitalism charges as Facebook, a company that never made any such promise. On Google, advertising now pushes organic search far down the page. Especially on mobile, you often scroll through pages of ads from national chains before you reach the site that has the best answer to your question. And in today’s AI-mode search, even the content is served up directly by Google, with far less traffic sent on to the sites that provide it. Likewise, Amazon, which used to call itself the most customer-centric company on earth, now puts sixteen ads and four organic results on a typical search results page. Sometimes, it may take scrolling past three screens of results to reach the first organic search result. And by “the first organic search result,” I mean “the best guess of the company’s smartest algorithms for what the user is actually looking for.” In former times, that was the top result. No more.

Industry observers note that the reason isn’t that good people turned bad. It’s in the overriding economic incentives of today’s shareholder capitalism. The extractive behavior the tech giants exhibit has been the norm for modern companies since Milton Friedman reset its objective in 1970, in a sentence that became doctrine: “The social responsibility of business is to increase its profits.” Harvard Business School, through the work of Meckling and Jensen, enshrined that view not only into corporate law but executive compensation. Whatever people’s original motives, the logic of the market eventually prevails, except in extraordinary cases. In his recent book Incorruptible, Eric Ries describes a set of institutions, norms, and guardrails that can help to safeguard the values of a company, but you can count on your fingers and toes the high profile companies that have successfully deployed them to resist the market. Even tax policy rewards capital appreciation by taxing it at a much lower rate than labor income.

Our corporations and the financial markets that govern them and reward them are a kind of machine, what the science fiction writer Charlie Stross calls a “slow AI.” We built it. We set its objective function to reward shareholders and ignore everyone else. And then we tell everyone that it is a marvelous self-correcting system. This is an illusion. As I put it in “We Have Already Let the Genie Out of the Bottle,” an essay I wrote for a Rockefeller Foundation workshop on regulating AI:.

Attempts at governance are futile until we recognize that we have built a machine and set it on its course. Instead, we pretend that the market is a natural phenomenon best left alone, and we fail to hold its mechanism designers to account. We need to tear down and rebuild that machine, reprogramming it so that human flourishing, not corporate profit, becomes its goal.

If the problem were just villains, you could fix things by firing them or shaming them or suing them or otherwise holding them to account. But if the problem is the design of the entire system, everyone is eventually incentivized to seek the same result. The machine rewards outsized growth of revenue and profit and brutally punishes any slowdown. Not only that, stock options tie every employee’s fortune to that reward.

Criticizing a firm for turning extractive isn’t really about the values of a company or the character of its executives and employees, it’s about the incentives that have been given to them.

Silicon Valley is a mirror of what’s wrong with our economy and our corporate governance, not the cause of it, and not even the worst exemplar. Tobacco, oil, pharma companies, and far too much of Wall Street vie for that spot. But Silicon Valley is a great place to study what went wrong, because companies rise and fall so swiftly, making them the equivalent of laboratory mice or flatworms, where patterns can be quickly identified and followed across generations.

A few years ago, I found a useful language for describing what I was seeing in the theory of economic rents.

The essential idea is that when the reward accruing to an actor is larger than their contribution to value creation, the difference is rent. To the classical economists, to Smith and Ricardo and Mill, living in a world of inherited privilege, rents were not a temporary aberration on the way to equilibrium. They were both a persistent consequence and a persistent source of inequality. Joseph Schumpeter had a different idea, that disproportionate profits can be a reward for innovation. An innovator can earn outsized profits during the expansive phase of a latest technology, when it’s solving new problems and creating value not just for consumers but for a whole ecosystem of suppliers and intermediaries and even competitors.

When economists talk about rent-seeking today, though, many of them mean what George Stigler called “regulatory capture” and what the public choice school built into its doctrine: rents extracted through government intervention at the behest of those who lobby officials and bureaucrats to get their way in despite the free market.

Recent findings suggest that the rents I want to talk about are a different animal. They are collected in the market, not around it, by private firms with enormous power, whose power is unchecked precisely because the government has stepped back.

For my purposes here, speaking about the rents that accrue to Silicon Valley companies, I divide them into two rough categories.

Recent findings suggest that the first is what I call rising tide rents. This fits with the classical idea of rent as a reward accruing to an actor that is larger than its contribution to value creation, but it is a virtuous kind, a kind of communal value creation, often the result of positive government interventions. Consider the rise in home prices that accrues to a homeowner who lives in a neighborhood that is improved by better schools or improved roads, which then may lead to new shops and restaurants or the home improvements made by neighbors. This is also a kind of unearned income. Everyone shares the improvements in quality of life. But homeowners get something bigger, the unearned income from the appreciation in home value.

In a recent development, in a similar way, leading companies make massive improvements to the neighborhood, so to speak, and we all benefit. I should point out that government plays a significant role in these improvements. It’s easy to forget the NSF grant that funded the research that became Google, the loan guarantees that made Tesla possible, and government as the founding customer for SpaceX’s commercial launch services. It’s a rising tide that lifts all boats, and the fact that the market leader takes the biggest share of it is not, to my mind, a scandal. But Schumpeter thought those outsized profits would eventually be competed away as knowledge diffuses through society. What is a scandal is the way that Business Strategy 101 and corporate governance today teach companies to build moats and barriers to keep profits high even when the company stops earning rewards by innovating and better serving customers.

Companies do this by turning to the second category of rents, which I call robber baron rents, the income above a competitive rate that gets collected because of asymmetries in power, the way the medieval baron’s troops collected their share of the harvest whether or not the baron had contributed anything to growing it.

The same firm can collect both kinds of rent at different stages in its lifecycle. As far as I can tell, the shift from one to the other is close to a law of the technology business cycle. The rising tide doesn’t last. Once the growth of a upcoming market slows, the now-powerful incumbents can no longer rely on new customers and a vibrant ecosystem to sustain their extraordinary profits. So they turn to extraction. They use their market power to hold on to their now-customary level of profit in the face of competition that ought to be eating it away. Cory Doctorow came up with a catchy name for this. He calls it enshittification.

There’s another problem with Silicon Valley and the economy writ large.

In a recent development, at one point in early 2021, when Elon Musk first became the richest person in the world, Bernie Sanders tweeted about it, contrasting Musk’s fortune with the frozen federal minimum wage. Bernie was right that the comparison was shocking. But he was wrong to imply that Musk’s wealth came from profits extracted at the expense of Tesla’s workers. The median Tesla worker makes considerably more than the median American worker, and up to that time, Tesla had few profits to extract. Musk didn’t hoard Tesla’s profits like a robber baron of old. He won a different kind of game.

According to recent reports, musk was paid in what the financial writer Jerry Goodman, writing under the pseudonym Adam Smith, called “supermoney.” The essence of Goodman’s insight is that any manufacturer that has been financialized through stock issuance is valued today as if it were already delivering the decades of future earnings reflected in its stock price. This is another of those ideas that help you to see the world in a fresh way. Once you realize that owners of capital are literally living in a different economy from those who earn income from their labor, you start seeing two different economies operating under two completely different sets of rules.

In a recent development, there’s the operating economy, where companies make and sell products and services and earn a profit by, as Nick Hanauer and Eric Beinhocker put it, solving human problems. And there’s the betting economy, where wealthy people bet on which companies will win the beauty contest that the stock market has become. In the operating economy, a dollar is a dollar. The neighborhood dry cleaner earns one dollar of profit and has that one dollar to spend. In the betting economy, a dollar of profit becomes many dollars of market value. At the time when Musk first became the world’s richest man, a dollar of Tesla profit turned into roughly $600 of stock market value. A dollar of Amazon profit at that time was worth about $67. A dollar of Google profit, about $34. The local business that isn’t financialized gets only $1.

That gap is one of the biggest unacknowledged drivers of inequality in this country, and it’s why one slice of society has gotten so much richer in recent decades while everyone else languished. Most rich people—and really, all holders of capital assets—live in the supermoney economy, where our assets are valued as if the future had already arrived and can be borrowed against, tax-free, today. This is the ultimate unearned income, or rent. Most everyone else lives in the dollar economy. If you’re a public-company executive paid in stock, or a venture capitalist, or an entrepreneur lucky enough to place in the financial horse race, you live in the other one, and you get a large interest-free loan from the future.

The betting economy, within reason, is a good thing. Speculative bets on the future are how we fund innovation and build infrastructure ahead of the prosperity it will bring. Tesla is a real company building real factories and real charging networks, and it kick-started a genuine transition to renewable energy. SpaceX and Starlink likewise required massive amounts of capital. And now AI has dwarfed even those bets.

Carlota Perez has shown that bubbles are a normal part of how revolutionary technologies get adopted. I’m not against betting. I’m worried about what we bet on, and what will be left over when the bubble pops.

According to recent reports, if your biggest lever for wealth creation is not in the market for real goods and services, but in the market for future expectations, it’s easy to continue down the slippery slope to making money by manipulating those expectations. And that’s the road Silicon Valley has charged down.

Industry observers note that sam Bankman-Fried captured the zeitgeist with his line “Number go up.” Silicon Valley has gotten addicted to value capture without value creation. Think about it: 75 to 80% of IPOs are for companies without any profits. Add in acquisitions of pre-IPO companies and the numbers are likely even worse. It’s like a horse race where bettors can collect their winnings when the horse has rounded the first or second turn.

There are still venture capitalists who look for companies that succeed by delivering real value to customers, but the prevalence of the profitless IPO has turned the venture-backed tech giant into a kind of financial instrument. Much as the bankers who invented the derivatives that nearly sank the global economy in the 2009 financial crisis eventually ran out of real mortgages to collateralize and turned to “liar loans” so they could keep the game going a little longer, the measure is no longer whether a company has a chance of living up to its promises but whether it can convince the investor in the next round that it can. Most startups are built to be refinanced all the way to the exit rather than to turn into sustainable businesses.

In a recent development, this dynamic is essential to the current AI infrastructure buildout. Data centers are built to meet expectations of massive future demand. But much of that demand is from companies that have not yet, as Silicon Valley used to describe it, found “product-market fit.” That is, they have not yet found customers willing to pay more than the product costs to deliver. In short, the future cash flows with which data center builders are expecting to pay back the trillions they have borrowed or invested are dependent on those customers’ ability to raise their next round at an ever-increasing valuation.

Recent findings suggest that AI is the real deal, a transformative technology like the internet. And its leading company, Anthropic, looks to be turning into an actual business with cash flow and profits. But others, even those like OpenAI with enormous revenues, are still dependent on massive additional capital infusions to survive. But it’s OK, as long as “number go up.”.

It has been revealed that A structure like this does not need demand to collapse. It only needs the hype to recede enough that it is no longer possible to raise more capital at ever more stratospheric valuations. That’s why we see hype in increasingly desperate amounts.

I first started thinking about this turn to hype in Silicon Valley in the days of Uber and Lyft. The innovation of using GPS and smartphones to create crowdsourced taxis on demand using people’s personal cars was real and crucial. But building the matching marketplace of riders and drivers took enormous subsidies, and it wasn’t terribly profitable. So Travis Kalanick, the CEO of Uber, told investors that Uber wasn’t out to replace taxis, but the private automobile. Then in the run-up to the IPO, he started talking about self-driving cars, presumably to suggest that Uber would be much more profitable once it was able to get rid of the cost of drivers. Meanwhile, Waymo kept its head down and did the hard work of actually building out the technology, which is only now coming to fruition.

According to recent reports, that kind of hype continued through the next one of Silicon Valley’s dry spells. There wasn’t much real innovation to talk about, so the masters of capital sold “the Metaverse” and eventually “Web3.” As the person who defined “Web 2.0,” I was asked frequently to opine on Web3. I tried to avoid answering. Most prognostications about the future turn out to be wrong. What we can do is ask questions that help us see the present more clearly. So finally, I laid out my reservations in a piece called “Why It’s Too Early to Get Excited About Web3.”.

Industry observers note that I explained how Carlota Perez and Bill Janeway distinguish productive bubbles from unproductive ones. In a productive bubble, speculative excess builds lasting infrastructure the future can capitalize on. The dotcom bubble was, in that sense, productive. When it popped, it left behind billions of miles of high-speed fiber and the data centers and the know-how that the next decade’s boom was built on. The 2009 mortgage bubble, on the other hand, left behind mostly wreckage.

In a recent development, the issue with Web3 wasn’t that the prices were crazy, since prices are always crazy in a bubble. It was whether anything was being built that would outlast the crash. What Silicon Valley delivered in that period mostly turned out to be betting with only the barest nod towards actual product. You probably all remember the craze for “bored apes.”.

Even when there is real substance to an investment bubble, Silicon Valley has learned to lean into hype as an instrument for drawing investment. For example, when Tesla’s stock began descending from the stratosphere, Elon Musk started touting humanoid robots as the future of Tesla and pitched SpaceX not on the basis of its actual business of commercial space launches and Starlink’s huge network of communications satellites, but on AI, and on promises of a self-sustaining city on Mars housing at least one million people, travel to any point on earth in 30 minutes, and a possible enterprise value of $100 trillion!

According to recent reports, not everyone can be as bold and imaginative as Elon Musk. But there’s one pretty sure bet that gets the investors to pile on, and that’s the promise of a monopoly.

Look no further than that race between Uber and Lyft. When they went toward their IPOs, neither was profitable, and their enormous valuations rested entirely on the premise that if you grow big enough and fast enough, profits will follow. Most monopolies and duopolies used to develop slowly and were understood as dangerous to competitive markets. Now Silicon Valley decided they are something to seek from the start, as the holy grail for investors. Reid Hoffman and Chris Yeh called this strategy Blitzscaling, a term they cheerfully derived from the Nazi blitzkrieg. Their argument is that you need to move fast enough to seize a market before anyone else can, even when you don’t yet know how you’ll make money. If you can promise a monopoly, you can raise a great deal of money.

I don’t have a blanket objection to moving fast. But do I think blitzscaling is a morally bankrupt idea, a game that defines winning as extracting value rather than creating it.

The saddest part of blitzscaling is that it has turned the original genius of the competitive market on its head. It’s now a kind of oligopoly of capital. Instead of customers choosing the winners, the VCs do it up front. Sunil Paul, the inventor of the technology and business model that Uber and Lyft soon dominated, raised only $35 million for his organization Sidecar, which was soon crushed when Uber and Lyft raised and spent billions on marketing and subsidized fares to quickly gain users.

If I had to name a villain in this transition, it would be Andreessen Horowitz. The firm was founded in 2009, at the start of the era of cheap capital I’ve been describing, and it built a media and narrative operation from the start. Benedict Evans, who worked there, later described the firm as “a media organization that monetizes through VC.” The story that a company will win because of how much money it has raised becomes part of how it actually wins. But I don’t think it allocates capital anything like as effectively as a well functioning market where customers pick the winners.

Industry observers note that what connects the enshittification of search, the supermoney economy, the blitzscaling of Uber, the narrative machine of a16z, and the crypto casino is not a run of bad actors. It’s shareholder capitalism reaching the late stage of its own logic. In its youth, that system was oriented, however imperfectly, toward creating value. In its endgame it has reoriented toward extracting it.

According to recent reports, we are standing at the beginning of the next turn of the cycle. This time, AI is the technology driving the boom. And once again, it represents the possibility of huge advances in human collective intelligence. Like the web was 25 years ago, it’s a new creative frontier enabled by technology.

Sources indicate that the pattern I described earlier usually has a rising-tide youth that comes before the extractive turn. However, in some ways, AI has been enshittified from the very beginning. It skipped the youth. The AI labs have taken in hundreds of billions of dollars, with trillions committed to data center buildout, and capital on that scale doesn’t wait for a business to grow into itself. It demands a return, and the pressure to repay it will inevitably push these companies toward value capture before they’ve finished creating value.

According to recent reports, AI also breaks the old bargain in a way even the enshittified web did not. Google, at its best, sent you somewhere else. It read the commons and pointed you back into it, 94% of the time without even trying to monetize it. AI doesn’t send you elsewhere at anything like the same rate. It offers a replacement for what you would once have gone out and found, an answer in place of the referral.

We’ve been told, again and again, that the secret of future prosperity is to create enormous, disproportionate rewards for innovators and their backers. The kind of people that tech companies used to serve as their customers don’t really matter. They are necessary casualties on the road to an unimaginably better future.

This is profoundly short sighted. An economy is a circulatory system. In The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, the visionary poet and painter William Blake (writing during the first Industrial Revolution) put the circulatory logic perfectly: “The Prolific would cease to be prolific unless the Devourer as a sea received the excess of his delights.” In other words: Output has to be consumed. The system has to flow.

Today, many AGI narratives assume that the “prolific” can keep producing and the broad mass of customers (“the devourer”) somehow continue to buy, even as more and more human labor is displaced and labor income and bargaining power collapses. That’s not a future of abundance. It’s a recipe for a kind of congestive heart failure for the economy.

If the AI labs wish to be architects of a prosperous future, they must work as hard on inventing the fresh economy’s circulatory system as they do on improving model capabilities. They need to measure success by diffusion, not just capability. They have to ask always how their customers are going to make money, not just how they themselves will. They have to treat the labor transition as a core problem to be solved, not just studied. They have to be willing to win in the marketplace, not through artificial moats. That means committing to open interfaces, portability, and interoperability. General-purpose capabilities should not become a private toll road.

It’s an economy crying out for mechanism design. Mechanism design is a term that I’ve shamelessly stolen from the economists and redefined to describe what I think is missing from the AI economy. It’s a branch of microeconomics that studies how to design the rules of a market in such a way that even self-interested actors who have private information are more likely to produce outcomes that are better for everyone. Leonid Hurwicz, the founder of the field, called it “reverse game theory” because it works backward from a desired outcome to develop the rules that will produce it.

They give Nobel prizes in economics for advances in the theory of mechanism design. But it seems to me that many of the most successful mechanism designs happen in the real world. They evolve. They are discovered. Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie weren’t trying to invent the marvelous open-ended game that we now call open source software when they designed Unix. They were just trying to build a portable operating system able to run on multiple hardware architectures. That also happened to mean that you could only distribute software via its source code rather than just the binaries. And their breakthrough design of a protocol-centric operating system with a small kernel surrounded by cooperating, communicating utilities created what I call “an architecture of participation.” Anyone could add to the system, or easily replace one of its standard parts with an alternative.

Recent findings suggest that that was a very different marketplace design than the proprietary operating systems of the day, which were created to tie software developers to specific hardware platforms. It led to a vibrant software sharing economy that is still going on today and that transformed all of software development.

You can see the same kind of evolution in AI. I don’t know that David Soria Parra and his colleagues at Anthropic meant to change the market structure of AI when they developed MCP, but that’s what happened. Rather than a winner-takes-most market in which developers call the APIs of the dominant, centralized platforms (as had happened previously with Windows for the PC, and iOs and Android for mobile), the agentic web began to take on the shape of the participatory economy of open source software and the web. People can bring their own models and infrastructure to the table as an alternative to the big centralized players. And that story is far from over. In fact, it is just beginning.

In a recent development, every major technology wave arrives in two stages. The first stage is the development of the technology itself: the personal computer, the World Wide Web, the smartphone, and now, generative and agentic and physical AI. The second stage involves the development of new economic mechanisms that enable transformative business models to take advantage of the technology. The earliest business models often imitate what went before and encode the business ambitions of the old technologies the creators grew up with. As the technology matures, the problems with the original business models become apparent, and eventually, through a process of trial, error, and invention, new mechanisms enable new business models.

Recent findings suggest that the web was invented in 1991. But the web advertising economy didn’t really take off until Google figured out PageRank, and then perfected pay-per-click advertising and the ad auction. Ecommerce didn’t take off until companies like PayPal made it safe to type your credit card number into a stranger’s website, and until Amazon built the warehousing and delivery networks that made rapid delivery possible. The smartphone put GPS in everyone’s pocket, but it wasn’t until Sunil Paul envisioned and built the first real-time location matching marketplace for ride sharing that Uber and Lyft and DoorDash were able to turn that capability into a huge on-demand economy. YouTube didn’t become the engine of the creator economy until it answered the takedown notices and lawsuits of the music industry not with stonewalling or settlements, but with Content ID.

Sources indicate that it’s easy to look at the winners, and think the path to get there was obvious. It wasn’t. There were all kinds of failed approaches to solving the problems that only became apparent during the technology diffusion and adoption period. I don’t have time to chronicle the graveyard of failed search, advertising, and ecommerce experiments and standards. But you don’t need to look back. Just look around. How many proposals there are today for managing rights, blocking or allowing bots, enabling agents to cooperate, and payment. There are at least six competing agent payment protocols alone. We’re in the exploratory phase of mechanism design for AI.

In a recent development, that’s where I come back to the idea of mechanism design as reverse game theory. Rather than asking ourselves the rules of the game we are now playing, it calls us to ask “What game ought we to be playing?” And that question leads me imperatively to my answer: “The game of human flourishing.”.

It has been revealed that we have been told that the game is the quest for superintelligence. We have been told it is a winner-takes-all game that will bring untold riches to the winners and impoverish everyone else. And we have seen mechanisms designed to support that game: massive investments in data center capacity such that only the well-capitalized can play, colonialist appropriation of existing intellectual property, closed model weights with terms of service that forbid others from learning from them, memory that locks our context inside one provider’s walls, and PR stunts like dumping millions of dollars of compute to solve high-profile math problems, or hyping the cybersecurity risks of their offerings, for which only their latest, most powerful models are offered as the only remedy.

In a recent development, if the game we want to play instead is human flourishing, we need to design mechanisms that lead us to that outcome. We need mechanisms that provide a circulatory economy of value exchange, for and by humans in partnership with AI, rather than replaced by it. And in my experience, those mechanisms look like open source, open protocols, open memory, because these are things that give the freedom for users to shape and control this most wonderful latest technology wave for ourselves.

Henry Farrell, Alison Gopnik, Cosma Shalizi, and James Evans argued in Science last year that large models are best understood not as independent intelligences but as a newly introduced kind of cultural and social technology, one that lets us take advantage of the information other humans have accumulated, in the lineage of pictures, writing, print, and internet search. AI may be the most powerful means of harnessing collective intelligence yet. The commons isn’t incidental to AI, it’s the material AI is made from.

In the world I see coming, AI is a medium, like painting or writing or music. If we get this right, everyone will get the same paints and brushes, the same words, the same notes, but some people draw more out of them than others, or do it better. We won’t decide up front that those who raise the biggest pool of capital are due all the rewards.

According to recent reports, our job is to draw something more, something better, out of the ocean of possibilities in the collected knowledge inside the model. AI was built from our collective intelligence. It should not be designed to replace us. It depends on us to create its value.

  • Mmathematician at Anthropic indicates he has used the company’s Claude AI model to prove the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic logo, Guilherand-Granges, France, March 2025.

Mmathematician at Anthropic indicates he has used the company’s Claude AI model to prove the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. Levent Alpöge made the claim in a note on his website on Friday, Bloomberg reported.

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote.

Recent findings suggest that the hypothesis, first proposed in 1859, concerns how prime numbers are spread out. It is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s seven Millennium Prize Problems, each of which carries a $1m prize. Alpöge notes his proof also covers a broader version, the generalised Riemann hypothesis.

In a recent development, he did not publish a traditional paper. Instead, he released the proof in Lean, a programming language that checks every logical step. The code runs to about 17 million lines, Science reported.

According to recent reports, andrew Sutherland, a senior research scientist at MIT, told Bloomberg he had checked the code on his own computer. He stated he had seen at least three other checks by professional mathematicians. Later on Friday, Sutherland put the chance that anything is wrong at roughly zero, Scientific American reported.

Recent findings suggest that however, other mathematicians urged caution. A proof that compiles in Lean still has to state the right problem, and humans have to confirm that it does.

Kevin Buzzard, a professor at Imperial College London, stated nobody yet understands what the proof shows, Al Jazeera reported. The proof has not been formally accepted.

Alpöge stated Claude did much of the work.

“This time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” he wrote.

Industry observers note that anthropic declined to comment to Bloomberg. The claim came a day after the organization’s record stock market debut.

Sources indicate that if confirmed, it would be the second Millennium Prize Problem that AI may have helped solve. In September, OpenAI remarked its models had produced a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem.

This webinar reveals how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. Popular secure messaging app Signal has rolled out a upcoming update that automatically disables screenshots for the sake of blocking Siri AI from reading your chats. Here are the details.

Signal’s latest app patch on iPhone disables a key system feature: taking screenshots.

As Signal told Reuters, that’s because Apple doesn’t currently provide better tools for iOS developers to safeguard app content from Siri AI and third-party AI agents.

By default, users who update and try to take a screenshot will see a message that claims: “Screenshot prevented by ‘Block Siri AI’ setting.”.

Fortunately, there’s an easy workaround. Owners who want to re-enable screenshots can do so by visiting Signal’s privacy settings and turning off the latest toggle that’s labeled ‘Block Siri AI.’.

While the black, gray and white colorways are the cheapest, some of the other more fun ones like matcha green and cherry blossom are also on sale too for $28.

Besides its sleek design and lightweight form factor, this Tomtoc carrying case also has a handle on top, cutouts for your Joy-Con's thumbsticks and game card slots for up to 12 games. Bringing your Switch 2 with you has never been easier or looked this good.

Although the Nintendo Switch 2 comes with 256GB of storage built-in, sooner or later you're definitely going to run out of space. While Nintendo's first-party games typically have small file sizes, bigger third-party titles like Cyberpunk 2077 or Split Fiction both take up over 60GB on their own. Fortunately, SanDisks' microSD Express Cards start as low as $49 at Amazon right now.

Industry observers note that while the 1TB version still costs a whopping $289 even after discounts, the 512GB and 256GB variants are much more affordable. And when it comes to storage, you can't go wrong with SanDisk which makes excellent microSD Express cards so you won't have to worry about losing your game downloads, saves and screenshots due to coruption.

Although it's reception didn't quite live up to the eight and half year wait, Metroid Prime 4 is still and amazing game and a real visual showcase on the Nintendo Switch 2. Right now, you can pick up Metroid Prime 4: Beyond for just $49 on Amazon and both the physical and digital versions are on sale.In my Metroid Prime 4: Beyond review, I praised its highly detailed levels, tight controls and combat and of course, it's stunning graphics on the Switch 2. I know trekking back and forth through the desert might be a turnoff for some but honestly, I really enjoyed how it broke up the action between levels and Samsus' motorcycle Vi-O-La handles quite well and is really fun to drive. If you're a returning Metroid Prime player or are fresh to this first-person shooter, now is the time to experience it at a steep discount.

Recent findings suggest that now if you don't like using the stock Joy-Cons on your Nintendo Switch or Switch 2, there are plenty of alternatives. However, with this controller, you aren't just limited to using it on your console as it always works with phones and smaller tablets too. Right now, you can grab the GameSir G8 Plus for just $59 on Amazon.

In the photo above and in our GameSir G8 Plus review, we tested the Thanos special edition but only the all-black version is right now on sale at Amazon. However, both the Thanos and Hulk versions of the GameSir G8 Plus are acually even cheaper at Walmart where you can pick up either for just $55.

Now admittedly, the Hori Piranha Plant Cam isn't the best webcam you can get for your Switch 2 but it's definitely the cutest. If you only use GameChat occasionally or just want to give that Nintendo gamer in your life something fun to unwrap, this could make for a nice gift and a great stocking stuffer.Right now, you can pick up the Hori Piranha Plant Cam for just $29 on Amazon. Alternatively, the Hori USB Camera is even cheaper at $24. While its picture quality is limited to just 480p, what I really like about the Hori Piranha Plant Cam is that the flower detaches from the base and you can use it in handheld mode too. In our Hori Piranha Plant Cam review, we praised its extremely cute design and I couldn't agree more. Just don't expect picture perfect image quality and you won't be disappointed.

It has been revealed that while Super Mario Party Jamboree was a lot of fun on the Switch, the Nintendo Switch 2 Edition of the game and its Jamboree TV expansion add some unique additions to the core Mario Party gameplay. You can literally put yourself in the game with the Nintendo Switch 2 Camera and play minigames using full-body motion controls, or play as others using Mouse Mode with the Switch 2 Joy-Cons.

It has been revealed that this package includes the Switch 2 hardware bundled with the flagship launch game, Mario Kart World. It retails for $449, which is $50 off. So if you were still on the fence about getting a Switch 2, this is your chance to save.

It has been revealed that donkey Kong Bananza is my favorite Switch 2 game, and it's now on sale for $20 off at Amazon! Explore (and destroy) a variety of imaginative worlds as you quest to reach the center of the planet. I particularly love the climax since it's such an awesome nod to the Donkey Kong Country games. This one comes with my high recommendation!

We've spotlighted this deal before, but it's worth repeating for those just seeing this post. This headset is already a steal at its normal price of $27, but for $14, it's virtually irresistible. It's worth a look if you want to level up the audio quality of the games you're playing on Switch 2.

If you're looking for another awesome kart racing game, look no further than Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds.

As we said in our Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds review, this spinoff in the Sonic the Hedgehog universe and part of the long-running racing series takes what Mario Kart games do well and improves on it. It’s the perfect blend of chaos and fun, introducing a ‘CrossWorlds’ mechanic that sees you thrown into a portal and onto another track mid-race. CrossWorlds poses a learning curve that’s oh-so-rewarding to master.

Sources indicate that I have a confession... I've never played Super Mario Galaxy! Blame it on not owning a Nintendo GameCube! But if you're like me, you can now get the games bundled together at a discount! You can play it on Switch 1 and Switch 2, but on the latter you get enhanced visuals.

In a recent development, the 8BitDo 64 is a lovable little gamepad for retro gaming on the PC, Switch, N64 and Analogue 3D. It brings the N64 control scheme up to modern standards without making too many compromises, and is perfect for playing retro Nintendo games. It’s affordable, hella cute, and packs decent battery life. My only qualms are that the layout can be a little awkward and the pad's scope is, by its very nature, limited. Don’t let either put you off.

Sticking with Capcom, you can also buy Pragmata on Switch 2 for $39. As I said in my Pragmata review, this unique action game combines puzzles with shooting. The story is also pretty endearing thanks to the adorable Diana. You won't want to miss it, as the Switch 2 version looks and plays like a dream.

Industry observers note that if you've somehow missed it, you can now get Resident Evil Requiem on the Switch 2 for $39! As I stated in my Resident Evil Requiem review, it's one of the best games of the year, thanks to its stunning graphics and terrifying gameplay. This game is not only a fantastic return to form, but also a great entry point for upcoming players.

Sources indicate that on our list of the best Nintendo Switch 2 controllers, the GameSir Super Nova is our favorite budget pick. Normally $49, the Super Nova has Hall effect triggers and thumbsticks, comes in two colorways and features back buttons, and has some great rumble haptics. We also liked its companion app that let us easily customize our experience. Our only major issue was that, with backlighting enabled, it lasted just six hours on a charge.

GameSir Super Nova: was $49 now $35 @ Amazon.

Recent findings suggest that does it run as well as it does on other consoles. No. But it's Elden Ring on the go — there's not much you could ask for than that. Apart from, oh. I dunno. A Black Friday deal that brings the price down to make it more affordable so that you can play it on your Switch 2 for less? Wish granted — it's got a $20 discount.

Sources indicate that filling up the storage space on a Switch 1 is super easy, and it's not much of a challenge on the more well-endowed Switch 2. That's where one of these comes in — you can add buckets of storage for even more games without breaking the bank. This SanDisk SD card will work perfectly with Switches, and it's on sale this Black Friday.

Looking for something a bit different? Strategy RPG Unicorn Overlord should scratch that retro itch while giving you plenty of modern gameplay conveniences. The story is deep and complex — and just look at that glorious art style. Perfect Black Friday purchase if you want something new to play.

In a recent development, I'm a huge Animal Crossing fan. Even though New Horizons is almost seven years old, I'd still recommend it to anyone with a Switch. It hasn't aged a day — the graphics are gorgeous, there's so much to do, and it's just the coziest, most comforting Switch game out there.

It has been revealed that it's ideal for kids (I first played Animal Crossing: Wild World on my Nintendo DS) and adults. You have to build your own island, make friends with your neighbors, and craft objects.

If you like cozy games and you haven't tried Animal Crossing, what are you doing?

While still outrageously expensive at $607 and with only $32 in savings, I guess every little bit helps when it comes to leveling up your gaming setup.

Right now, you can get The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and a Nintendo Switch 2 for $607, down from $639. As I said earlier, the Switch deals haven't really started to trickle in yet, so we gotta make do with what we're given.

Recent findings suggest that these days, I can only play Mario Kart for about four races before my hand starts cramping. The tiny Switch Joy-Cons are just too small for my hands! I need to play with a controller; otherwise I'm useless and in pain before the end of the Grand Prix/World Tour.

The NEXT racing wheel is compatible with both the original Switch and the Switch 2, and right now it's $8 down from $11.

Oh, and don't forget that you get 2 — so you're paying $4 per wheel.

I remember spending hours playing Mario Party after school, and now Super Mario Party Jamboree brings even more excitement. This game is suitable for both kids and adults, so it could be a friends hangout entertainment or even a cozy family night.

Sources indicate that the now-immortalized Super Mario Galaxy game is discounted from $69 to $49. Compatible with both the Switch original and Switch 2, this platformer takes you on a cosmic adventure with Rosalina.

You get Super Mario Galaxy and Super Mario Galaxy 2 included, so you're kind of getting two games for the price of one.

Right now, the Switch and Switch 2 Black Friday game deals are few and far between. Of course, games like Kirby and Donkey Kong are discounted, but we've yet to spot any savings on Mario Kart World, which has been $79 since its release.

But it's been a hard year — it would be nice for Nintendo to reward us for getting through it with some unprecedented Mario discounts (hint, hint).

Which games would you like to see discounted?

Why spend $500 on a Nintendo Switch 2 just to throw it in your backpack and risk it getting wet, scratched, cracked, or worse? The NEXT Switch 2 has a padded outer shell and contains game storage pockets for on-the-go gaming, worry-free.

In a recent development, although technically a Switch original game, Donkey Kong Country Returns is supported on the Switch 2. This platformer game sees you hunting for bananas, destroying obstacles, and swinging on vines.

It's available for $41 down from $59.

It has been revealed that we reviewed the Turtle Beach Airlite headset last year and awarded it a near-perfect 4.5-star rating, praising its clear mic and lightweight feel. Although it's wired only, if you game with your Switch handheld, this will be a non-issue.

It has been revealed that right now, save $24 on Kirby and the Forgotten Land Switch 2 version, or save $18 on the original Switch version. This whimsical game sees you inhaling enemies (yes, literally) to save your friends.

Industry observers note that do you have Kirby and the Forgotten Land on Switch but want to play it on Switch 2? Nintendo has discounted the upgrade pack from $19 to $13, so you can carry on playing on your Switch 2 for cheaper.

Recent findings suggest that although Nintendo Switch 2 deals are pretty slim pickings at this point in the deal cycle, Resident Evil Requiem is currently $20 off at Best Buy. This zombie game is the Resident Evil franchise's ninth entry and features both first- and third-person perspectives.

I'm sure you already have Animal Crossing: Newly introduced Horizons, which came out almost seven years ago (yep, I'm old...). But what new stuff can scratch the ACNH itch? I've found this Turtle Beach Switch 2 controller with two iconic Animal Crossing characters: Tom Nook with his beady landlord eyes (he's always watching you...) and K. K. Slider with his enchanting guitar.

Right now, this controller is 15% off — $42 down from $49.

Although we're still technically five days out from the big day, most Black Friday sales have dropped now. However, it doesn't look like any Switch 2 consoles are discounted. I wish I came bearing better news!

Even so, you can grab the Nintendo Switch 2 + Mario Kart World for $499 (down from its MSRP of $549). Again, I'm sorry this isn't a better deal, but Nintendo hasn't reduced the price of any of its consoles.

According to recent reports, my colleagues and I play Mario Kart World every Wednesday, and it's the highlight of my week. Mario Kart World is overwhelming chaos but I love it anyway.

Basketball fans, NBA 2K27 is the latest entry in 2K's long-running sports series, giving you plenty of ways to get stuck into the action. You can create your own player and work towards NBA stardom in MyCAREER, build a dream team in MyTEAM or take charge of a franchise in MyNBA.

Industry observers note that there's also The City, where you can team up with friends and compete across different courts. The Switch 2 version also includes motion-controlled mini-games, which offer something a little different from the usual matches. It's worth bearing in mind that you'll need a fair bit of storage space for this one, too, with the download weighing in at 83.2GB. But at just $29 right now over at Amazon, you can't go wrong.

Sonic X Shadow Generations brings two adventures together, with a remastered version of Sonic Generations alongside a brand-new campaign starring Shadow. You'll get to revisit some familiar stages as Sonic, while Shadow's story introduces new abilities, boss fights and plenty of nods to his history in the series.

In a recent development, we enjoyed it when we reviewed the game, awarding it four stars in our review, so seeing it drop from $49 to just $19 at Amazon is a decent saving. That's 61% off the original price, making it a much easier purchase to justify if you've been meaning to give it a go.

According to recent reports, A gaming headset doesn't have to cost a fortune, and the Turtle Beach Airlite Fit is a relatively simple option for Nintendo Switch players. It's a wired headset, so you won't have to worry about charging it between gaming sessions, and it connects through a standard 3.5mm audio jack. It features 40mm speakers, a flip-to-mute microphone for chatting with friends and an onboard volume control.

The over-ear design also has cushioned ear pads (although I'd keep expectations in check if you're after something with more premium features). It's compatible with the Nintendo Switch 2, original Switch and Switch Lite, making it an option worth considering if you're shopping on a tighter budget, especially now that it's just $14 at Amazon.

If you're looking to upgrade your Nintendo Switch 2 setup, the PDP Afterglow is a great accessory to add to your wishlist. Its translucent design and customizable RGB lighting give the controller plenty of personality, with four preset lighting modes and adjustable brightness to help you find a look you like. There's more to it than flashy lights though. TMR thumbsticks are designed to deliver precise, responsive controls while reducing the risk of stick drift, and you also get built-in motion controls and two programmable back buttons.

There's even a dedicated C Button for quick access to Nintendo Switch 2's GameChat features. With wireless connectivity and up to 40 hours of battery life per charge, it's a handy alternative to your standard Joy-Con controllers. Plus, you can over 50% off right now, with PDP Afterglow now priced at just $24 at Amazon.
